import coil.compose.rememberAsyncImagePainter
import com.example.musicapp.Data.Artist
import com.example.musicapp.Data.Category

@Composable
fun ArtistsDetailScreen(
    genre: Category,
    artists: List<Artist>,
    onArtistSelected: (Artist) -> Unit = {},
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier
) {
    Column(modifier = modifier) {
        Text(
            text = "Genre Artists: ${genre.name}",
            style = MaterialTheme.typography.h6,
            modifier = Modifier.padding(start = 16.dp, end = 16.dp, top = 16.dp, bottom = 8.dp)
        )

        LazyVerticalGrid(
            columns = GridCells.Fixed(2),
            contentPadding = PaddingValues(16.dp)
        ) {
            items(artists) { artist ->
                ArtistItem(artist, onArtistSelected)
            }
        }
    }
}

@Composable
private fun ArtistItem(artist: Artist, onClick: () -> Unit) {
    Surface(
        modifier = Modifier
            .padding(8.dp)
            .clickable(onClick = onClick)
            .aspectRatio(1f),
        shape = RoundedCornerShape(8.dp),
        elevation = 4.dp,
        border = BorderStroke(width = 1.dp, color = Color.LightGray)
    ) {
        Box(
            modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize()
        ) {
            val painter = rememberAsyncImagePainter(model = artist.picture_medium)

            Image(
                painter = painter,
                contentDescription = artist.name,
                contentScale = ContentScale.Crop,
                modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize()
            )

            Text(
                text = artist.name,
                modifier = Modifier
                    .align(Alignment.BottomCenter)
                    .background(color = Color.Black.copy(alpha = 0.7f))
                    .fillMaxWidth()
                    .padding(4.dp),
                style = MaterialTheme.typography.body2,
                color = Color.White, // Change the text color to white
                textAlign = TextAlign.Center
            )
        }
    }
}

            Vector2 velocity = PhysicsUtils.velocityToPosition(body, target, maxSpeed);
            body.setLinearVelocity(velocity);


I want the velocity to slow down gradually in relation to the distance between current body position and target. Velocity should slow down more as the position gets closer to target. I want to control this with an Interpolation function.

This method should be able to smoothly push a body with it’s returned velocity even when the distance to target is very small like 0.01f

deltaTime,
PhysicsSystem.STEP_FREQUENCY (when physics timestep = 1/60f, this = 60f)
float maxSpeed (in meters per second)
Vector2 targetPosition

conversation.content: html for audio tag do i have to type in the type

Yes, it's best practice to include the `type` attribute in the `audio` tag. The `type` attribute specifies the MIME type of the audio file and helps the browser determine how to handle the audio data. By providing the correct `type` attribute value, you can ensure that the audio plays back correctly on all browsers and devices.

Here's an example of how to include the `type` attribute in the `audio` tag:

```html
<audio controls>
  <source src="audio.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
  <source src="audio.ogg" type="audio/ogg">
  Your browser does not support the audio element.
</audio>
```

In this example, we include two `source` elements with different file formats and MIME types. The browser will choose the first source element that it is able to play back based on its capabilities. If neither source element is supported, the fallback text "Your browser does not support the audio element." will be displayed.

Note that the `type` attribute value should match the MIME type of the audio file. You can find a list of MIME types for common audio formats here: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Basics_of_HTTP/MIME_types/Audio_and_video_types

The issue is likely because the `fetchArtistDetails` function in your `ArtistsViewModel` returns a single `ArtistDetail` object but sets the value of the `_artistDetails` `MutableStateFlow` to `artistDetail`. You need to set the value to a list containing the `artistDetail`. Replace this line in your `fetchArtistDetails` function:

```kotlin
_artistDetails.value = artistDetail
```

with:

```kotlin
_artistDetails.value = listOf(artistDetail)
```

Additionally, you have a small issue in the `ArtistsScreen` composable with the artist selection navigation. Replace this line:

```kotlin
navController.navigate("artistDetail/{artist.id}")
```

with:

```kotlin
navController.navigate("artistDetail/${artist.id}")
```

After applying these changes, you should no longer see an empty page and the `ArtistDetailScreen` should show up correctly.

package com.example.tradingchecklist

import android.content.Context
import android.view.LayoutInflater
import android.view.View
import android.view.ViewGroup
import android.widget.CheckBox
import androidx.recyclerview.widget.RecyclerView
import kotlinx.android.synthetic.main.checklist_item.view.*

class ChecklistAdapter(private val context: Context) :
    RecyclerView.Adapter<ChecklistAdapter.ViewHolder>() {
    
    private val dummyChecklist = listOf(
        ChecklistItem("Criteria 1", 50),
        ChecklistItem("Criteria 2", 25)
    )

    override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int): ViewHolder {
        val view = LayoutInflater.from(context).inflate(R.layout.checklist_item, parent, false)
        return ViewHolder(view)
    }

    override fun getItemCount(): Int {
        return dummyChecklist.size
    }

    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: ViewHolder, position: Int) {
        holder.bind(dummyChecklist[position])
    }

    inner class ViewHolder(itemView: View) : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(itemView) {
        fun bind(item: ChecklistItem) {
            itemView.checklist_text.text = item.text
            itemView.percentage.text = item.percentage.toString()
            itemView.check_criteria.setOnCheckedChangeListener(null)
            itemView.check_criteria.isChecked = item.checked
            itemView.check_criteria.setOnCheckedChangeListener { _, isChecked ->
                item.checked = isChecked
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Protocol is SSL
1. Diffie Hallman key exchange
2. RSA authentication
3. AES encryption

And for secure server connection cipher suite configuration
1. Protocol is SSL

To satisfy these requirements, Ram can use the following cipher suite configuration for his client and server programs:

For the secure client connection, he should use:

`SSL_DH_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA256`

This configuration has the following properties:
1. Diffie-Hellman key exchange
2. RSA authentication
3. AES encryption with a 256-bit key in CBC mode
4. SHA-256 message digest

For the secure server connection, he should use:

`SSL_DH_anon_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA512`

This configuration has the following properties:
1. Diffie-Hellman key exchange
2. No authentication (anonymous)
3. Triple DES encryption (3DES) with EDE (Encrypt, Decrypt, Encrypt) mode and CBC
4. SHA-512 message digest

Please note that using "anonymous" authentication is considered less secure because it allows for potential man-in-the-middle attacks. However, you're not mapping the necessary album information when you get the API response. To fix this issue, you need to update your `DeezerRepository` class to map the album data properly:

1. In `DeezerApiService`, replace the `ArtistDetailResponse` line with the following:

data class AlbumResponse(

    val coverBig: String,
    val coverXl: String,

```

3. Update the `getArtistDetail` function in the `DeezerRepository` class:

```kotlin
suspend fun getArtistDetail(artistId: Int): ArtistDetail {
    val response = deezerApiService.getArtistDetail(artistId)

    // Map album data
    val albums = response.albums?.map { albumResponse ->
        Album(
            id = albumResponse.id,
            title = albumResponse.title,
            link = albumResponse.link,
            cover = albumResponse.cover,
            coverSmall = albumResponse.coverSmall,
            coverMedium = albumResponse.coverMedium,
            coverBig = albumResponse.coverBig,
            coverXl = albumResponse.coverXl,
            releaseDate = albumResponse.releaseDate,
            tracklist = albumResponse.tracklist,
            type = albumResponse.type
        )
    }

    return ArtistDetail(id = response.id, name = response.name, pictureBig = response.picture_big, albums = albums)
}
```

By making these changes, you should now be able to view the album image and release date on the artist's detail screen.

)

import com.example.musicapp.Data.AlbumDetails
// other imports

class DeezerRepository {
    // existing methods

    suspend fun getAlbumDetails(albumId: Int): AlbumDetails {
        val response = deezerApiService.getAlbumDetails(albumId)
        return AlbumDetails(
            id = response.id,
            title = response.title,
            cover_medium = response.cover_medium,
            songs = response.tracks.data

}

To create a token management system in MySQL, you can start by creating the following tables:

1. `users` - to store user information
2. `tokens` - to store token details
3. `token_bookings` - to store token booking details

Here is the SQL code to create these tables:

```sql
-- Create the users table
CREATE TABLE users (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    first_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    last_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Create the tokens table
CREATE TABLE tokens (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    description TEXT,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Create the token_bookings table
CREATE TABLE token_bookings (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    token_id INT NOT NULL,
    booking_date DATE NOT NULL,
    booking_time TIME NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id),
    FOREIGN KEY (token_id) REFERENCES tokens (id)
);
```

These tables will allow you to create a token booking management system where users can book tokens, and you can store their booking information. The_foreign_key_constraints_ensure_proper_relationships_between_the_tables_and_restrict_invalid_operations.

Sure, here's an example of using the created tables for a token booking management system. Let's insert some sample data into the `users` and `tokens` tables and then create a booking using the `token_bookings` table.

1. Insert sample data into the `users` table:

```sql
INSERT INTO users (first_name, last_name, email, password_hash)
VALUES ('John', 'Doe', 'john.doe@example.com', 'hashed_password');
```

2. Insert sample data into the `tokens` table:

```sql
INSERT INTO tokens (name, description)
VALUES ('Token A', 'This is a description for Token A.');
```

3. Create a booking for the user and token:

```sql
INSERT INTO token_bookings (user_id, token_id, booking_date, booking_time)
VALUES (1, 1, '2022-12-01', '10:00:00');
```

4. Query the database to get the booking details along with user and token information:

```sql
SELECT CONCAT(u.first_name, ' ', u.last_name) AS user_name, 
       u.email AS user_email, 
       t.name AS token_name, 
       t.description AS token_description, 
       tb.booking_date, 
       tb.booking_time
FROM token_bookings tb
JOIN users u ON tb.user_id = u.id
JOIN tokens t ON tb.token_id = t.id;
```

This query will return a result similar to:

|-----------|----------------------|------------|---------------------------|--------------|--------------|
| John Doe  | john.doe@example.com | Token A    | This is a description for Token A. | 2022-12-01   | 10:00:00     |

question : “Companies these days now have the option to control their users very well owing to the
introduction of token management systems that possess a well-developed database.
Features needed –
● This definitely assists in handling tokens in a more simple way
● Novices should get acquainted with this as it is one of the best SQL project ideas
they can begin with.”
make tables for token booking management system in mysql server code dbms


1. query to retrieve the no. Of tokens assigned to a user.
2. To retrieve the token status of  any particular user, how many token genarated by that uaser and which tokens are expire.
3. updation on token tables with insertion of a new user.
4. view on the output of ex 1
5. list of all users who have tokens < say 3

etc.

To create the tables and implement the requested queries, I will assume that there are two main tables: a `users` table and a `tokens` table. Here's the MySQL code to create these tables:

1. Creating the `users` and `tokens` tables:

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  username VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE tokens (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  user_id INT NOT NULL,
  token VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  expires_at TIMESTAMP,
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
);
```

2. Query to retrieve the number of tokens assigned to a user:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS tokens_count FROM tokens WHERE user_id = ?;
```
Replace the '?' with the desired user's ID.

3. To retrieve the token status of any particular user (how many tokens generated, which tokens are expired):

```sql
SELECT tokens.*, 
       (expires_at < NOW()) AS is_expired 
FROM tokens 
WHERE user_id = ?;
```
Replace the '?' with the desired user's ID.

4. Insertion of a new user and creation of a new token:

```sql
INSERT INTO users (username, email) VALUES ('John Doe', 'john.doe@example.com');
SET @new_user_id = LAST_INSERT_ID();
INSERT INTO tokens (user_id, token, expires_at) VALUES (@new_user_id, 'example-token', DATE_ADD(NOW(), INTERVAL 1 DAY));
```

5. Creating a view for the output of the token count query (example for user with ID 1):

```sql
CREATE VIEW user_tokens_count AS
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS tokens_count
FROM tokens
GROUP BY user_id;

SELECT * FROM user_tokens_count WHERE user_id = 1;
```

6. List of all users who have less than a specific number of tokens, e.g., 3 tokens:

```sql
SELECT users.*
FROM users
JOIN user_tokens_count ON users.id = user_tokens_count.user_id
WHERE user_tokens_count.tokens_count < 3;
```

3. Test the Image composable with a static image URL: In the AlbumDetailItem composable, try using a static URL for the song image to verify if the issue is with the Image composable or the data source.

4. Log the song.cover_medium before displaying the Image composable: You can add a log statement in the AlbumDetailItem composable to print the song.cover_medium value before displaying the Image. This can help you find out if the value is null or an incorrect URL.

If you find any issues with the data or the mapping, you can fix those issues accordingly.

```kotlin
val painter = rememberAsyncImagePainter(model = song.cover_medium)
```

With:

```kotlin
val painter = rememberImagePainter(
    data = song.cover_medium,
    builder = {
        crossfade(true)
        transformations(CircleCropTransformation())
        placeholder(if (song.cover_medium == null) R.drawable.placeholder else 0)
    }
)
```

This will add a placeholder, enable crossfade, and apply a circle crop transformation while loading the image.

Make sure to import the required dependencies:

```kotlin
import coil.compose.rememberImagePainter
import coil.transform.CircleCropTransformation
```

And add an appropriate placeholder image in your drawable resources (e.g., R.drawable.placeholder).

Check if these modifications resolve the issue with the image not being displayed in the AlbumDetailItem composable.

### Issue 1 - Unresolved reference

This issue is caused due to an incorrect import. To resolve this, make sure that you have the correct import as shown below:

```kotlin
import androidx.compose.runtime.collectAsState
```

### Issue 2 - Type mismatch

In the `PlayerViewModel` class, you should replace

```kotlin
private val _favorites = mutableStateOf<List<Song>>(emptyList())
```

with

```kotlin
private val _favorites = mutableStateOf(emptyList<Song>())
```

And make sure to import this:

```kotlin
import androidx.compose.runtime.mutableStateOf
```

### Issue 3 - 'create' overrides nothing

Change the `PlayerViewModelFactory` class to the following (make sure the class extends ViewModelProvider.NewInstanceFactory instead of ViewModelProvider.Factory):

```kotlin
import android.content.Context
import androidx.lifecycle.ViewModel
import androidx.lifecycle.ViewModelProvider

class PlayerViewModelFactory(private val context: Context) : ViewModelProvider.NewInstanceFactory() {
    override fun <T : ViewModel?> create(modelClass: Class<T>): T {
        if (modelClass.isAssignableFrom(PlayerViewModel::class.java)) {
            return PlayerViewModel(context) as T
        }
        throw IllegalArgumentException("Unknown ViewModel class")
    }
}
```

The problem here is that you're trying to use the `hiltViewModel` function in a non-Hilt enabled Composable function. The `hiltViewModel` function is resolved from the `androidx.hilt.navigation.compose` package, which requires Hilt Navigation Compose library. To fix this issue, follow these steps:

1. Add the Hilt Navigation Compose library to your `build.gradle` (app level) file.

```groovy
dependencies {
    // other dependencies

    implementation 'com.google.dagger:hilt-navigation-compose:1.0.0-alpha03'
}
```

2. In your Composable function, import `hiltViewModel`:

```kotlin
import androidx.hilt.navigation.compose.hiltViewModel
```

Now the `hiltViewModel` function should resolve correctly, and the error should be gone. Remember to sync your project after adding the library to the `build.gradle` file.

Building an API documentation using Swagger (now known as OpenAPI) and Node.js can significantly improve the developer experience by providing an interactive and easy-to-understand documentation of your API. Here's a step-by-step guide on how to create API documentation using Swagger and Node.js:

1. Set up a Node.js project:

Create a new directory for your project and navigate to it in the terminal. Next, initialize a new Node.js project by running:

```
npm init
```

Install the required dependencies:

```
npm install express --save
npm install swagger-ui-express --save
npm install yamljs --save
```

Create a new file `app.js`:

```
touch app.js
```

2. Create a basic Express server:

Redacting the `app.js`, add the following code to initialize a basic Express server:

```javascript
const express = require('express');
const app = express();
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.send('Hello World!');
});

app.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`Server is listening on port ${port}`);
});
```

3. Add Swagger UI to your server:

In `app.js`, add the following code to import and configure Swagger UI:

```javascript
const swaggerUi = require('swagger-ui-express');
const YAML = require('yamljs');
const swaggerDocument = YAML.load('./swagger.yaml');

app.use('/api-docs', swaggerUi.serve, swaggerUi.setup(swaggerDocument));
```

This code imports the Swagger UI Express module, loads the `swagger.yaml` configuration file (which we will create in the next step), and sets up a new route `/api-docs` for the Swagger UI.

4. Create API definition using OpenAPI in a `swagger.yaml` file:

In the project folder, create a new file named `swagger.yaml`:

```
touch swagger.yaml
```

Open the `swagger.yaml` file and start defining your API, following the OpenAPI Specification. Here is a basic example:

```yaml
openapi: "3.0.0"
info:
  version: 1.0.0
  title: Sample API
  description: A sample API documentation using Swagger and Node.js

servers:
  - url: http://localhost:3000
    description: Local development server

paths:
  /:
    get:
      summary: Get hello message
      operationId: getHelloMessage
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Success
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  message:
                    type: string
                    example: Hello World!
```

5. Test your API documentation:

Now that you have your API defined in the `swagger.yaml` file and your Express server is set up, you can start your server by running:

```
node app.js
```

Navigate to `http://localhost:3000/api-docs` in your web browser to view and test your interactive API documentation powered by Swagger UI.

Remember, you can always extend and update your `swagger.yaml` to include new endpoints, request and response types, and other API configurations.

The global clustering coefficient algorithm is a measure used in graph theory and network analysis, which helps to determine the overall level of clustering or interconnectedness in a network. It quantifies how much nodes tend to cluster together and how likely it is for a node's neighbors to also be connected to each other. It can be useful for understanding the structure and robustness of a network, as well as predicting the potential spread of information or infection within the network.

The global clustering coefficient can be computed using the following steps:

1. Compute the local clustering coefficient for each node:

    The local clustering coefficient of a node is the proportion of its neighbors that are also connected to each other. It is determined by calculating the ratio between the number of existing links (E) between a node's neighbors and the maximum number of possible links (M) between those neighbors.

    Local clustering coefficient (C_i) for node i = E / M

2. Average the local clustering coefficients of all nodes:

    Compute the mean of all local clustering coefficients to get the network's global clustering coefficient. This will give an overall sense of the interconnectedness of the network.

    Global clustering coefficient (C) = (Sum of all C_i) / N

    where N is the number of nodes in the network.

Alternatively, the global clustering coefficient can be calculated using the following formula:

Global clustering coefficient (C) = (3 * total number of triangles) / total number of connected triples

Here, a triangle is a set of three nodes, each connected to the other two, and a connected triple is a set of three nodes where at least two are connected to the third one.

The value of the global clustering coefficient ranges from 0 to 1. A high global clustering coefficient value indicates a dense network with many interconnected nodes, while a low value indicates a sparse network with fewer connections between nodes.

To calculate the global clustering coefficient using the formula mentioned earlier, you will need to first identify the number of triangles and connected triples in the network. Given a set of nodes and edges, you can follow these steps:

1. Create an adjacency matrix:
Create a square matrix (n x n) where 'n' is the number of nodes in the network. Set the value in row 'i' and column 'j' to 1 if there is an edge between the nodes 'i' and 'j', and set it to 0 if there's no edge. Make sure to set the diagonal to 0 as there should be no self-loops. This adjacency matrix (let's call it A) will help you identify triangles and connected triples more easily.

2. Calculate A^3:
Compute the cube of the adjacency matrix (A^3). When you multiply the adjacency matrices, the resulting A^3 matrix will contain the information about all possible paths of length 3 between nodes.

3. Count the number of triangles:
The diagonal of the A^3 matrix (elements A^3[i, i] for i = 1 to n) will give you the number of triangles that include node 'i'. You will then sum up these diagonal elements and divide by 6 (since each triangle is counted for each of its three nodes and counted twice due to the ordering of nodes) to obtain the total number of triangles (T).

Total number of triangles (T) = (Sum of diagonal elements of A^3) / 6

4. Count the number of connected triples:
To find the total number of connected triples, you need to calculate the total number of reachable triples and then subtract the count of triangles. Calculate the sum of degrees of all nodes (degree is the number of edges attached to a node). Then, for each node, subtract 1 from its degree and divide the result by 2. Sum up all the values you get. This is the number of reachable triples. Now, subtract the triangles you already counted in step 3.

Total number of connected triples (Tr) = (Sum of reachable triples) - (3 * Total number of triangles)

5. Calculate the global clustering coefficient:
Now that you have the number of triangles (T) and connected triples (Tr), you can calculate the global clustering coefficient (C) using the formula:

Global clustering coefficient (C) = (3 * total number of triangles) / total number of connected triples

Global clustering coefficient (C) = (3 * T) / Tr

This will give you an overall measure of the interconnectedness of the network considering the given nodes and edges.

If you only have the total number of edges and total number of nodes, you cannot directly calculate the global clustering coefficient without more information about the network structure. The clustering coefficient depends on the specific arrangement of these edges between nodes, as well as the triangles and connected triples within the network.

C_expected = ⟨C_i⟩ ≈ ⟨k⟩ / N

where N is the total number of nodes.

But it's important to note that this approach only approximates the global clustering coefficient based on average degree; it doesn't provide an accurate value for the actual network, which depends on its specific topology (i.e., the arrangement of edges between nodes).                 }
            }
        )
    }

formula of global clustering coefficient using only triangles and connected triplets

The formula for the global clustering coefficient using only triangles and connected triplets is given by:

Global Clustering Coefficient = (3 * Number of Triangles) / Number of Connected Triplets

Here, the number of triangles refers to the number of closed triplets in the graph, and the number of connected triplets refers to the total number of triplets having at least one connection between the nodes involved. The coefficient represents how densely the nodes cluster together to form a closed loop in the graph. The factor of 3 accounts for the ways to choose the central node in each possible triplet.

conversation.content: why I cannot see any typeerors in node terminal in react

You may not see any TypeScript errors in the Node.js terminal while running a React app because of webpack's `watch` mode. 

In `watch` mode, webpack recompiles the app as you make changes, but the TypeScript errors will only show up in the terminal if you change a file that is actually being watched by webpack. If you only change a file that is not being watched (e.g. a type definition file), the errors won't appear in the terminal until you make a change to a watched file.

In addition, if you have set up your TypeScript configuration to ignore errors by using the `noEmitOnError` option in your tsconfig.json file, then the TypeScript errors won't prevent webpack from building the app. This may result in an app with silent errors. 

To avoid this, you should ensure that `noEmitOnError` is set to `true` in your tsconfig.json file, and double-check that the files that you're working on are being watched by webpack. 

You can also check the browser console when running the app to see any type errors that may occur at runtime.

why there are not any webapack files in react default app?

By default, the create-react-app tool generates a pre-configured development environment for you that includes everything you need to start building a React app with minimal setup. This includes a pre-configured webpack configuration that handles common tasks such as bundling, transpiling, and optimizing your code without you needing to manually configure webpack yourself.

The create-react-app tool abstracts away the complexity of the webpack configuration by hiding the configuration files in its own npm package (react-scripts). This package provides a set of pre-configured webpack configurations for different environments (development, production, testing, etc.) that are optimized for React-based applications. 

The webpack configuration files are generated when you run the `npm start` command to start the development server or when you run the `npm run build` command to generate a production build. 

You can also override the default configuration settings by running the `eject` command, which exposes the configuration files in your project and allows you to customize the webpack configuration to your specific project needs. However, this is not recommended unless you know exactly what you're doing and have a good reason for doing it, as ejecting from create-react-app is a one-way operation that cannot be undone.

sudo apt-get install google-chrome-stable

const browser = await puppeteer.launch({

});

const newArray = originalArray.filter(callback);

- `index` (optional): The index of the current element being processed in the array.

conversation.content: in sql server, is there a way to get the entire chain of foreign keyed tables starting from a specific table?

In SQL Server, there isn't a built-in query to get the entire chain of foreign keyed tables starting from a specific table. However, you can use Common Table Expressions (CTE) and system catalog views to achieve this. 

Here's a script that does this:

```sql
-- Replace 'YourTableName' with the starting table name you want to find the chain for
DECLARE @TableName NVARCHAR(128) = 'YourTableName';

WITH CTE_FK_Chain (ParentTable, ParentColumn, ReferencedTable, ReferencedColumn, Level)
AS (
    -- Base case: Get tables directly referenced by the starting table
    SELECT 
        OBJECT_NAME(fk.parent_object_id) AS ParentTable,
        COL_NAME(fkc.parent_object_id, fkc.parent_column_id) AS ParentColumn,
        OBJECT_NAME(fk.referenced_object_id) AS ReferencedTable,
        COL_NAME(fkc.referenced_object_id, fkc.referenced_column_id) AS ReferencedColumn,
        1 AS Level
    FROM sys.foreign_keys fk
    INNER JOIN sys.foreign_key_columns fkc ON fkc.constraint_object_id = fk.object_id
    WHERE OBJECT_NAME(fk.parent_object_id) = @TableName

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive case: Keep finding tables referenced by the current Table
    SELECT 
        OBJECT_NAME(fk.parent_object_id),
        COL_NAME(fkc.parent_object_id, fkc.parent_column_id),
        OBJECT_NAME(fk.referenced_object_id),
        COL_NAME(fkc.referenced_object_id, fkc.referenced_column_id),
        c.Level + 1
    FROM sys.foreign_keys fk
    INNER JOIN sys.foreign_key_columns fkc ON fkc.constraint_object_id = fk.object_id
    INNER JOIN CTE_FK_Chain c ON c.ReferencedTable = OBJECT_NAME(fk.parent_object_id)
)

SELECT * 
FROM CTE_FK_Chain
ORDER BY Level;
```

This will give you the chain of foreign keyed tables in a hierarchical format, starting from the specified table. The `Level` column indicates the depth of the foreign key relationship.

If you are using the `react-intersection-observer` library with Jest and getting a `ReferenceError: IntersectionObserver is not defined` error, it's likely because Jest doesn't provide a global `IntersectionObserver` object by default.

Fortunately, there's an easy solution to this problem. 

1. First, install the `intersection-observer` package as a dev dependency:

```
npm install --save-dev intersection-observer
```

2. In your test setup file (e.g. `jest.setup.js`), define `IntersectionObserver` as a global object using `require`:

```javascript
global.IntersectionObserver = require('intersection-observer');
```

3. In your Jest configuration (e.g. `jest.config.js`), specify the test setup file:

```javascript
module.exports = {
  // other config settings
  setupFilesAfterEnv: ['./jest.setup.js'],
};
```

This will configure Jest to use the `intersection-observer` package and provide a global `IntersectionObserver` object for your tests.

With this fix, you should no longer get the `ReferenceError: IntersectionObserver is not defined` error when testing `react-intersection-observer` components with Jest.

2. **Build the ASSIMP library:**

   ASSIMP uses CMake as its build system. First, ensure that you have CMake installed on your system. You can download CMake from https://cmake.org/download/.

3. **Create a build directory:**

   Inside the "assimp" folder, create a new folder called "build". You can do this by running:

   ```
   cd assimp
   mkdir build
   cd build
   ```

4. **Configure the build using CMake:**

   Run the following command to configure the build:

   ```
   cmake ../
   ```

   By default, the CMake configuration will try to build a dynamic version of the library. If you want to build a static version, you can use the following command instead:

   ```
   cmake -DASSIMP_BUILD_STATIC_LIB=ON ../
   ```

conversation.content: How do module scripts work?

Module scripts in Roblox are script objects that contain reusable code or data. They are similar to regular scripts, but instead of running immediately, they can be loaded and used by other scripts. 

When a module script is required by another script, its code is executed only once. The module script's return value is then cached, and any subsequent calls to that module script from other scripts will return the cached value. This allows developers to create libraries of functionality that can be easily shared between multiple scripts or projects.

Module scripts can contain any Lua code, including functions, tables, and variables. To export functionality from a module script, developers can use the `return` statement at the end of the script to specify the values they want to make available to other scripts. 

To require a module script in another script, developers can use the `require` function followed by the path to the module script relative to the current script. For example, if a module script named "mymodule" is located in ReplicatedStorage, a script that wants to use it would use `require(game.ReplicatedStorage.mymodule)`.

Overall, module scripts allow for better code organization and reusability in Roblox game development.
Can you change the module script's values in another script?

Module scripts in Roblox are fundamentally read-only. Once a module script returns its values to the requiring script, those values cannot be modified by the requiring script. 

However, if the module script returns a table or other reference type rather than a primitive value (like a boolean or number), it is possible to modify the properties of that table by the requiring script. For example, if a module script returns a table with properties, like this:

```lua
local myModule = {}

myModule.value = 5

return myModule
```

Then the requiring script can modify the values of the properties of that table, like this:

```lua
local myModule = require(game.ReplicatedStorage.myModule)

myModule.value = 10
```

However, it is generally considered bad practice to modify values returned by a module script, as it can lead to unexpected behavior that is difficult to debug. Instead, values returned by a module script should be treated as immutable and any necessary changes should be made within the module script itself.
Can I also change string values?

No, you cannot change the string values returned by a module script. Strings are immutable data types in Lua, which means that once they are created, their values cannot be modified. Any attempts to modify a string will actually create a new string object with the modified value.

Module scripts that return string values should therefore be treated as read-only, and any necessary modifications should be made within the module script itself.

If you need to use a string value that can be modified by another script, you can consider using a shared StringValue object instead. StringValue objects are Roblox Instances that can be created and modified in-game, and can be used to share string values between scripts. However, because they are Roblox Instances, they are subject to replication latency and can lead to race conditions if multiple scripts attempt to modify the same StringValue object simultaneously. Therefore, it is important to be careful when using shared StringValue objects and always handle potential synchronization issues.

In SQL Server, a view is a virtual table that is based on the result set of a SELECT statement. A view consists of rows and columns, just like a table, but its data comes from one or more tables. You can create a view as a way to simplify or customize the presentation of data from multiple tables, combine data from multiple tables, or abstract the underlying table schema.

Here are several queries demonstrating the different ways views can be created using the provided employees and departments tables:

1. Create a view that shows the employees' full names, hire dates, and salaries:

```sql
CREATE VIEW employee_full_name_and_salary AS
SELECT first_name + ' ' + last_name AS full_name, hire_date, salary
FROM employees;
```

2. Create a view that shows the total salary for each department:

```sql
CREATE VIEW department_total_salaries AS
SELECT d.department_id, d.name AS department_name, SUM(e.salary) AS total_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_id, d.name;
```

3. Create a view that shows the average salary for each department:

```sql
CREATE VIEW department_average_salaries AS
SELECT d.department_id, d.name AS department_name, AVG(e.salary) AS average_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_id, d.name;
```

4. Create a view that shows the employees' full names along with their department names and locations:

```sql
CREATE VIEW employee_department_info AS
SELECT e.first_name + ' ' + e.last_name AS full_name, d.name AS department_name, d.location AS department_location
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;

5. Create a view that shows the employees' full names, hire dates, and salaries, but only for employees who have a salary higher than a certain amount (e.g., 60000):

```sql

FROM employees
WHERE salary > 60000;
```

These are just a few examples of views that can be created using the provided tables. You can create more views by modifying the conditions, grouping, and aggregations in the SELECT statements, or by joining the tables in different ways. Remember that views can be queried just like regular tables, and you can also use them in other views or sub-queries.

    }, []string{"pod_name"})
)

conversation.content: Cannot acquire a schema lock because of an existing lock

A schema lock is a type of lock in a database management system that prevents other users from accessing or modifying the schema of a database (e.g. adding new tables, modifying existing ones, or altering relationships).

If you are receiving an error message that states "Cannot acquire a schema lock because of an existing lock", it means that another user or process has already acquired a schema lock on the database, and as a result, you cannot make any changes to the schema until the lock is released.

To resolve this issue, you can try the following steps:

1. Wait for the current user or process to release the schema lock. Depending on the complexity of the operation that is being performed, the lock may be held for several minutes or longer.

2. Identify the user or process that has acquired the schema lock, and contact them to ask them to release the lock. You may need to work with your database administrator or IT department to identify the user or process.

3. Restart the database management system. This can help to release any existing locks and allow you to acquire a new schema lock.

4. If none of the above steps work, you may need to perform a database backup, then perform a restore to recreate the database schema. This should only be done as a last resort, as it can be a time-consuming process and may result in data loss.

It's important to note that acquiring schema locks is a necessary part of database management, as it helps to ensure data integrity and prevent conflicts between multiple users or processes. However, if you frequently encounter schema lock issues, it may be a sign that your database schema needs to be reorganized or optimized to reduce contention.

conversation.content: What is the regex pattern to exactly match a word?

The regex pattern to exactly match a word is `\bword\b`, where "word" is the word you want to match. This pattern will only match the exact word and not any partial words or words that contain the searched word as a substring. The "\b" represents a word boundary which ensures that the searched word is not part of a larger word or connected to another character without a space or punctuation.
How to match the exact string with regex javascript

To match an exact string using regex in JavaScript, you can use the `test()` method or the `match()` method.

Method 1: Using the `test()` method

You can use the `test()` method of the RegExp object to test if a string matches the pattern. The `test()` method returns a Boolean value indicating whether the string matches the pattern or not.

Here's an example:

```javascript
let pattern = /exact string/i; // The "i" flag makes the search case-insensitive
let str = "This is an Exact string.";
let isMatched = pattern.test(str); // Returns true if the pattern matches the string
```

Method 2: Using the `match()` method

You can use the `match()` method of the string object to get an array of all substrings that match the pattern. The `match()` method returns `null` if no matches are found.

Here's an example:

```javascript
let pattern = /exact string/i; // The "i" flag makes the search case-insensitive
let str = "This is an Exact string.";
let matches = str.match(pattern); // Returns an array of all matches found
```

Note: You can replace the word "exact string" in the examples above with the string you want to match.

how to generate boundary with only numbers

According to the RFC 2046 standard, the boundary string for multipart/form-data must consist of 70 or more characters from a set of characters that are legal in ASCII printable characters. This includes alphanumeric characters, along with a few other characters such as '_' (underscore), '-' (hyphen) and '.' (period).

Here's a simple function to generate a random boundary string consisting of only numbers with a specified length:

```python
import random
import string

def generate_numeric_boundary(length=16):
    chars = string.digits
    return ''.join(random.choice(chars) for _ in range(length))
```

You can use this function to generate a random boundary string consisting of only numbers and pass it along with the Content-Type header in your POST request:

```python
boundary = generate_numeric_boundary()
headers = {
    'Content-Type': 'multipart/form-data; boundary=' + boundary
}
```

Note that using only numbers to generate the boundary string may not be valid according to the standard. It's recommended to use a combination of alphanumeric characters, along with other valid characters like '_' (underscore), '-' (hyphen) and '.' (period) to ensure it's a valid boundary string.

To save a large JSON data (including 200,000 records) into a CSV file in Python, you can use the built-in `json` and `csv` libraries.

Here's an example code that loads JSON data from a file, flattens the data, and writes it to a CSV file:

```python
import json
import csv

# Load JSON data from file
with open('data.json', 'r') as f:
    data = json.load(f)

# Flatten the JSON data
flat_data = []
for record in data:
    flat_record = {}
    for key, value in record.items():
        if isinstance(value, dict):
            for subkey, subvalue in value.items():
                new_key = f"{key}_{subkey}"
                flat_record[new_key] = subvalue
        else:
            flat_record[key] = value
    flat_data.append(flat_record)

# Retrieve column headers from the first record
headers = flat_data[0].keys()

# Write the flattened data to a CSV file
with open('data.csv', 'w', newline='') as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=headers)
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(flat_data)
```

This code first loads the JSON data from a file called `data.json`. It then flattens the data by converting nested dictionary values into separate columns. This is done using a loop that iterates over each record in the data set.

The flattened data is then written to a CSV file called `data.csv`. The code first retrieves column headers from the first record in the flattened data set. It then creates a `csv.DictWriter` object that writes the data to a CSV file. The `writeheader()` method is called to write the column headers to the first row of the CSV file, followed by the `writerows()` method to write the rest of the data rows.

Note that since you're dealing with a large data set, it may be more efficient to stream the data from the JSON file and write it to the CSV file in smaller chunks, rather than loading the entire data set into memory at once.

Yes, Pandas provides a variety of data cleaning methods in addition to filtering out incomplete records using `dropna()`. Here are some common data cleaning methods that you can use in Pandas:

### 1. Data type conversion

Use the `astype()` method to convert data types of columns. For example, to convert a column of strings to integers:

```python
df['string_column'] = df['string_column'].astype(int)
```

### 2. Removing duplicates

Use the `drop_duplicates()` method to remove duplicate rows. You can specify which columns to check for duplicates using the `subset` parameter. For example, to remove duplicate rows based on the 'name' and 'age' columns:

```python
df.drop_duplicates(subset=['name', 'age'], inplace=True)
```

### 3. Renaming columns

Use the `rename()` method to rename columns. For example, to rename the 'old_name' column to 'new_name':

```python
df.rename(columns={'old_name': 'new_name'}, inplace=True)
```

### 4. Handling missing values

Use the `fillna()` method to fill missing values. You can fill missing values with a specific value or use a method like 'ffill' or 'bfill' to forward-fill or backward-fill missing values. For example, to fill missing values in the 'age' column with the mean age:

```python
df['age'].fillna(df['age'].mean(), inplace=True)
```

### 5. Removing outliers

Use the `quantile()` method to find and remove outliers. For example, to remove rows with values outside of the 95th percentile of the 'age' column:

```python
df = df[df['age'] <= df['age'].quantile(0.95)]
```

These are just a few examples of data cleaning methods available in Pandas. You can also use methods like `replace()`, `fillna()`, and `drop()` to handle invalid data, remove or fill missing values, and remove irrelevant columns.

This function is used for regular copy operations where the original value of `other` is preserved. Therefore, it is the `operator=(const Parent& other)` that makes the `Parent` class assignable and helps to create a new instance of `Parent` using an existing one.

In summary, `operator=(const Parent& other)` creates a new instance of `Parent` using an existing one without modifying the original instance, which makes it suitable for copy operations. If the `UAbilitySystemBlueprintLibrary::SendGameplayEventToActor()` function is not starting the ability on your local player, there might be several reasons for this. Let's go through some potential issues and their solutions:

1. Incorrect Gameplay Tag on the ability or event
Make sure that the `GameplayTag` of the event you're sending matches the `GameplayTag` of the ability trigger that you've set up. The ability's `FGameplayAbilitySpec::ActivationInfo` struct contains a `StartAbilityTriggerData` member, which holds a `TriggerTagName`. To fix this, double-check both the event and the ability tags and correct inconsistencies.

2. Ability is blocked
The ability system might be blocking the ability execution. Some possible reasons for this are the ability is on cooldown, the player doesn’t have enough resources or meets other conditions in the custom `CanActivateAbility` function or `CheckCost`. Check for the possibility of blocked ability execution.

3. Problems with Ability System Component
Ensure that the Ability System Component setup is correct for the player character. The player should have an Ability System Component (ASC) in their Actor, and the ASC should be initialized correctly and have granted abilities. Additionally, the ASC should be bound to the input, which may be invoked by the Gameplay Cues.

You can try adding logs or breakpoints to the following methods to help trace your issue: 
- `UAbilitySystemComponent::HandleGameplayEvent(FGameplayTag EventTag, const FGameplayEventData *Payload)`
- `UAbilitySystemComponent::InternalTryActivateAbility(FGameplayAbilitySpecHandle AbilityToActivate, FGameplayAbilityActorInfo *ActorInfo, FGameplayAbilityActivationInfo ActivationInfo, const FGameplayEventData *TriggerEventData, FGameplayTag ApplicationTag)`

Also, make sure to check the logs in the Output Log tab for any warnings during runtime, as they might provide hints to the root cause of your problem.

4. Network Replication Issues
If your project supports multiplayer, there may be issues with network replication. Verify that the `GameplayTags`, the Ability System Component, and the necessary Events are correctly replicated and initialized on client-side actors.

Remember that these are general guidelines to help troubleshoot, and there could be other reasons specific to your project. Make sure to carefully follow the Unreal Engine Gameplay Ability System setup and double-check each step.

`Declare your template class as inline` analyze the pros and cons of this behaviour.

Declaring a template class as inline has the following pros and cons:

Pros:
- Ensures that the template code is generated in every translation unit that uses it, so the constructor will always be called.
- Reduces the potential for linker errors and can simplify the build process.
- Can improve performance by reducing function call overhead, especially for small functions or those called frequently.

Cons:
- May increase the size of the executable, since the generated code will be duplicated in multiple translation units.
- Can increase compilation time, since each compilation unit has to regenerate the code for the template class.
- Can lead to code bloat, since every instance of the template class will generate a copy of the code, even if only a few of those instances are actually used.

Overall, declaring a template class as inline can be a useful technique for ensuring that its constructor is always called, particularly in situations where initialization order is critical. However, it should be used judiciously, since it can increase code size and compilation time if overused.

is there a way to force link source files to produce static library using cmake script

Yes, there is a way to force link source files to produce a static library using a CMake script. 

In your CMake script, you can use the `set_target_properties()` command to set linker flags that will force the inclusion of specific object files in the final static library. Here's a sample CMake code that demonstrates how to do this:

```
add_library(my_library STATIC
  my_module_a.cpp
  my_module_b.cpp
)

# Force inclusion of object files in the static library
set_target_properties(my_library PROPERTIES
  LINK_FLAGS "-Wl,--whole-archive $<TARGET_OBJECTS:my_library> -Wl,--no-whole-archive"
)
```

This code creates a static library called "my_library" containing the source files "my_module_a.cpp" and "my_module_b.cpp". The `set_target_properties()` command is then used to set linker flags that will force the inclusion of all object files in the final static library, even if they're not used explicitly.

Please note that this technique should be used with care, and only when you have a good reason to force the inclusion of certain object files. If you can structure your code differently to avoid using this technique, that's usually a better option.

Yes, you can use SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) images in Jetpack Compose. To use SVG images, you need to add the `androidx.compose.foundation:foundation-svg` dependency to your project. You can do this by adding the following line to your app module's `build.gradle` file:

```kotlin
dependencies {
    implementation "androidx.compose.foundation:foundation-svg:<compose_version>"
    // other dependencies
}
```

Once you have added the dependency, you can use the `Image` composable to display SVG images. Here is an example:

```kotlin
import androidx.compose.foundation.Image
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.fillMaxSize
import androidx.compose.runtime.Composable
import androidx.compose.ui.Modifier
import androidx.compose.ui.graphics.painter.Painter
import androidx.compose.ui.res.painterResource
import androidx.compose.ui.res.useResource

@Composable
fun MyComposable() {
    val svgPainter: Painter = painterResource(id = R.drawable.my_svg_image)
    Image(
        painter = svgPainter,
        contentDescription = "My SVG Image",
        modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize()
    )
}
```

In the example above, we are using the `painterResource` function to load the SVG image from the resources. You can also use the `useResource` function to load the SVG image and cache it, so that it can be reused later without being reloaded from the resources. Note that the SVG image must be located in the `res/drawable` or `res/raw` directory of your project.

conversation.content: what is interface segregation principle

The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) is a principle of object-oriented design that states that a class should not be forced to implement interfaces that it doesn't use. The ISP is one of the SOLID design principles and aims to improve the flexibility, maintainability, and scalability of software systems.

According to the ISP, clients should not be forced to depend on methods that they do not use. Instead, interfaces should be designed to be specific to the needs of the clients that use them. This means that interfaces should be small and focused, with methods that are relevant to a single area of functionality.

By adhering to the ISP, we can create software systems that are easier to change and extend over time. This is because classes are not burdened with unnecessary dependencies on methods that they don't use, which reduces the risk of unintentional side effects when changes are made.

For example, suppose we have an interface that defines methods for handling customer orders, customer support, and customer billing. Instead of having a single interface, we could create three separate interfaces, each with its own set of methods. This would allow clients to implement only the interfaces they need, without being forced to depend on methods they don't use.

In summary, the Interface Segregation Principle advocates for designing interfaces that are specific to the needs of clients, with a focus on small and focused interfaces that are easy to change and extend over time.

The `equals()` method in Java is a method that is inherited from the `Object` class and is used to check if two objects are equal. 

In the expression `Integer.class.equals`, the `equals()` method is used to check if the `Integer` class object is equal to another object. The other object in this case is not specified, which means that the method will return `false` as the class object cannot be equal to an undefined object.

The `equals()` method in Java is typically used to compare the values of objects to determine if they are equal. For example:

```
Integer a = 5;
Integer b = 5;
System.out.println(a.equals(b)); // true
```

In this example, the `equals()` method is used to compare the values of `a` and `b` to determine if they are equal. Since both `a` and `b` have the same integer value of 5, the method returns `true`.

```

In this example, we create an `Integer` object `a` with a value of 5. We also create an `Object` reference `b` that is initialized with an `Integer` object using the `valueOf()` method.

To check if `a` is equal to `b`, we call the `equals()` method on `a` and pass in `b` as the argument. The method returns `true`, indicating that the two objects are equal.

The error messages you're encountering are due to Content Security Policy (CSP) restrictions. The extension is blocking inline JavaScript execution and media requests with the `data:` protocol.

To fix these issues, follow these steps:

1. Create a separate JavaScript file, e.g., `popup.js`, and move the inline `onclick` JavaScript code from the HTML file to the new JavaScript file:

`popup.js`:
```javascript
document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', () => {
  const clearDataButton = document.getElementById('clear-data-button');
  clearDataButton.addEventListener('click', clearData);
});
```

2. Replace the `onclick` attribute on your `<svg>` tag with an `id` attribute:

```html
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="clear-data-button" x="0px" y="0px" viewBox="0 0 512 512" style="enable-background:new 0 0 512 512; cursor:pointer;" xml:space="preserve">
...
</svg>
```

3. Add `<script src="popup.js"></script>` to the end of the `body` tag in your `popup.html` page:

```html
...
</body>
<script src="popup.js"></script>
</html>
```

4. If you still have issues with the `media-src` directive, update your CSP to allow `data:` sources. However, first, check if the provided changes have been effective. 

This approach will help you conform to the Content Security Policy rules by removing inline JavaScript and setting up a separate event listener in an external JavaScript file.

what is the properre dimension for icons in firefox? 16x16px or 32x32px?

Firefox supports various icon sizes for different use cases. For instance, the most recommended sizes for extension icons are 16x16px, 32x32px, and 48x48px. However, it's a good idea to provide additional sizes such as 64x64px or 96x96px, in case high-resolution displays require larger icons.

Thus, the recommended sizes for icons in Firefox are:

- 16x16px for small icons, like toolbar icons
- 32x32px for medium icons, like page action or browser action icons
- 48x48px for extension icons in the Add-ons Manager

You can provide multiple icon sizes in your `manifest.json` file like this:

```json
{
    "manifest_version": 3,
    "name": "Your Extension Name",
    "version": "1.0",
    ...
    "action": {
        "default_icon": {
            "16": "icon16.png",
            "32": "icon32.png",
            "48": "icon48.png"
        },
        ...
    },
    ...
}
```

In Laravel, you can use the `required_without` validation rule to indicate that a field is required when none of the listed fields are present. If you want to specify that a field should be required when any one of the listed fields are not present, you can use the `required_without_all` validation rule instead.

Here's an example of how to use the `required_without_all` validation rule in a Laravel validation rule:

```php
$request->validate([
    'email' => 'required_without_all:phone,fax',
]);
```

In this example, the `email` field is required if neither the `phone` nor `fax` fields are present. If either the `phone` or `fax` field is present, the `email` field is no longer required.

You can use the `|` operator to specify multiple validation rules for a given field. For example:

```php
$request->validate([
    'email' => 'required_without_all:phone,fax|email',
]);
```

This example requires that the `email` field is present and is a valid email address if neither the `phone` nor `fax` fields are present.

Note that the `required_without_all` rule only checks if any of the fields in the list are missing from the request. If any field in the list is present, even if it has a blank value, the rule will pass. If you want to require that all of the listed fields are missing, you can use the `required_without_all` rule instead and specify `*` as the parameter. For example:

```php
$request->validate([
    'email' => 'required_without_all:*',
]);
```

This would require the `email` field to be present if all other fields are missing from the request.

```php
use Jenssegers\Mongodb\Eloquent\Model;

}

use App\Models\ApiRequest;

public function storeRequestAndResponse(Request $request)
{

    $responseBody = 'Your custom response logic';

conversation.content: The detailed steps to do ETL with example codes in Snowflake

ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) is a process that involves extracting data from various sources, transforming it into a suitable format, and loading it into a database or data warehouse. Snowflake, a cloud data warehouse, has the capability to perform ETL tasks efficiently. Here's an example of how you can perform ETL using Snowflake:

1. Extract: Read data from an external source (e.g., a CSV file in an S3 bucket)

First, create a stage object in Snowflake to access S3:

```sql
-- Create storage integration
CREATE STORAGE INTEGRATION s3_integr
TYPE = EXTERNAL_STAGE
STORAGE_PROVIDER = S3
ENABLED = TRUE
STORAGE_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::<account_id>:role/<role_name>'
STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS = ('s3://your-s3-bucket/');
```

```sql
-- Create a stage object
CREATE STAGE my_stage
URL = 's3://your-s3-bucket/data/'
STORAGE_INTEGRATION = s3_integr
FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE=CSV);
```

2. Transform: Transform the extracted data into the desired format, usually specific to the target database or data warehouse schema.

In Snowflake, you can create a table and run SQL transformations:

```sql
-- Create a destination table
CREATE TABLE my_table (
  id INTEGER,
  name STRING,
  age INTEGER,
  city STRING
);
```

3. Load: Load the transformed data into the target database or data warehouse.

In Snowflake, use the COPY INTO command to load data from the stage to the destination table:

```sql
-- Load data from stage to the table
COPY INTO my_table
  FROM (
    SELECT
      t.$1::INTEGER as id,
      t.$2 AS name,
      t.$3::INTEGER as age,
      t.$4 AS city
    FROM @my_stage t
  )
  FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE=CSV)
  ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';
```

Now you have successfully performed the ETL process in Snowflake by extracting data from a CSV file in an S3 bucket, transforming it as per the target table schema, and loading it into the Snowflake table.

Remember that this is just an example. In a real-world scenario, you may need to perform more complex transformations using SQL queries or even use a third-party ETL tool like DBT, Matillion, or Fivetran.

Unfortunately, SQL update operations cannot conditionally update to a different value depending on some criteria; they can only update a specific column(s) with a specific value or a derived value from the same row.

However, the following SQL illustrates how to set the ticket status for tickets assigned to an agent with a specified last name:

```sql
DECLARE @AgentLastName NVARCHAR(30) = 'Smith';
DECLARE @AgentID INT;
SET @AgentID = (SELECT AgentID FROM Agent WHERE LastName = @AgentLastName);

-- Assign an existing status to the ticket if it's the first ticket for an agent
WITH TicketStatus_CTE AS (
    SELECT TicketID,
           COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY AgentID) AS NumTickets
    FROM Ticket
    WHERE AgentID = @AgentID
)

UPDATE Ticket
SET TicketStatusID = (
    SELECT TicketStatusID
    FROM TicketStatus
    WHERE Status = 'Specific Status' -- specify the status that should be assigned
)
FROM Ticket
JOIN TicketStatus_CTE ON Ticket.TicketID = TicketStatus_CTE.TicketID
WHERE AgentID = @AgentID AND TicketStatus_CTE.NumTickets = 1;

-- If another ticket is assigned to the same agent, set another status
UPDATE Ticket
SET TicketStatusID = (
    SELECT TicketStatusID
    FROM TicketStatus
    WHERE Status = 'In asteptare pentru ' + QUOTENAME(@AgentLastName)
)
FROM Ticket
JOIN TicketStatus_CTE ON Ticket.TicketID = TicketStatus_CTE.TicketID
WHERE AgentID = @AgentID AND TicketStatus_CTE.NumTickets > 1;
```

This query first checks if the agent has exactly one ticket assigned. If so, update the status of that ticket to a specified status. If the agent has more than one ticket assigned, update the status of subsequent tickets to "In asteptare pentru agent_name". Here are 10 views based on the provided database schema, with individual requirements for each view:

1. View all orders with customer details:

```sql
CREATE VIEW OrdersWithCustomerDetails AS
SELECT o.OrderID, c.CustomersID, c.FirstName, c.LastName, o.Order_date, o.Shipped_date
FROM Orders o
JOIN Customers c ON o.CustomersID = c.CustomersID;
```

2. View all products with their categories:

```sql
CREATE VIEW ProductsAndCategories AS
SELECT p.ProductID, p.ProductName, cat.CategoryID, cat.CategoryName
FROM Products p
JOIN Categories cat ON p.CategoryID = cat.CategoryID;
```

3. View all tickets with the assigned agent's name and ticket status:

```sql
CREATE VIEW TicketDetails AS
SELECT t.TicketID, t.Subject, t.Description, a.FirstName AS AgentFirstName, a.LastName AS AgentLastName, ts.Status
FROM Ticket t
JOIN Agent a ON t.AgentID = a.AgentID
JOIN TicketStatusHistory tsh ON t.TicketID = tsh.TicketID
JOIN TicketStatus ts ON tsh.TicketStatusID = ts.TicketStatusID;
```

4. View supplier products and details:

```sql
CREATE VIEW SupplierProductDetails AS
SELECT sp.SupplierID, s.CompanyName, sp.ProductID, p.ProductName
FROM Supplier_product sp
JOIN Suppliers s ON sp.SupplierID = s.SupplierID
JOIN Products p ON sp.ProductID = p.ProductID;
```

5. View all closed tickets with their resolution time (difference between CreatedDate and UpdatedDate):

```sql
CREATE VIEW ClosedTicketsWithResolutionTime AS
SELECT t.TicketID, t.Subject, t.Description, t.CreatedDate, t.UpdatedDate,
       DATEDIFF(DAY, t.CreatedDate, t.UpdatedDate) AS ResolutionTimeInDays
FROM Ticket t
JOIN TicketStatusHistory tsh ON t.TicketID = tsh.TicketID
JOIN TicketStatus ts ON tsh.TicketStatusID = ts.TicketStatusID
WHERE ts.Status = 'Closed';
```

6. View all orders with their respective shipper's details:

```sql
CREATE VIEW OrdersWithShippers AS
SELECT o.OrderID, o.Order_date, o.Shipped_date, s.ShipperID, s.CompanyName
FROM Orders o
JOIN Shippers s ON o.ShipVia = s.ShipperID;
```

7. View the average rating for each product:

```sql
CREATE VIEW ProductAverageRating AS
SELECT p.ProductID, p.ProductName, AVG(r.Rating) AS AverageRating
FROM Products p
JOIN Review r ON p.ProductID = r.ProductID
GROUP BY p.ProductID, p.ProductName;
```

8. View the total sales amount for each customer:

```sql
CREATE VIEW CustomerTotalSales AS
SELECT c.CustomersID, c.FirstName, c.LastName, SUM(od.UnitPrice * od.Quantity) AS TotalSalesAmount
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o ON c.CustomersID = o.CustomersID
JOIN Order_Details od ON o.OrderID = od.OrderID
GROUP BY c.CustomersID, c.FirstName, c.LastName;
```

9. View all products that have been discontinued:

```sql
CREATE VIEW DiscontinuedProducts AS
SELECT ProductID, ProductName, CategoryID, UnitPrice, UnitsInStock
FROM Products
WHERE Discontinued = 1;
```

10. View all agents and the count of tickets assigned to them:

```sql
CREATE VIEW AgentTicketCount AS
SELECT a.AgentID, a.FirstName, a.LastName, COUNT(t.TicketID) AS AssignedTicketCount
FROM Agent a
LEFT JOIN Ticket t ON a.AgentID = t.AgentID
GROUP BY a.AgentID, a.FirstName, a.LastName;
```

Integrating the Nordic nRF Connect SDK's nRF9160 driver into a generic Zephyr SDK project requires several steps. Please note that nRF7002 seems to be an incorrect part number, so I will be using the nRF9160 as the example.

2. Clone the appropriate repositories:
To use the nRF Connect SDK with Zephyr, you'll need the following repositories:
   - nrf (Nordic Semiconductors' additions, patches, and sample-codes for Zephyr)
   - nrfx (Hardware Abstraction Layer libraries from Nordic Semiconductors)
   - zephyr repository from Nordic Semiconductor

Use the `west` tool to initialize and clone the repositories. You can find the instructions on initializing and setting up the nRF Connect SDK environment in the following guide:

https://developer.nordicsemi.com/nRF_Connect_SDK/doc/1.7.0/nrf/doc/legacy/static/ug_ncs.html

3. Create a new Zephyr project:
Create a new directory for the project, and add a `CMakeLists.txt` and a `prj.conf` file. In the `CMakeLists.txt` file, remember to include the `zephyr` directory and the file `FindPackageZephyr` cmake function.

Example `CMakeLists.txt` content:

```
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.13.1)

find_package(Zephyr REQUIRED HINTS $ENV{ZEPHYR_BASE})
project(my_project)

target_sources(app PRIVATE src/main.c)
```

4. Configure the project to use the nRF9160 driver:
In the `prj.conf` file, add the configuration variables for the nRF9160 driver and any other required configurations:

```
# Enable nRF9160 driver
CONFIG_MODEM_NRF9160=y
```

5. Update the source code:
In the `src/main.c` file, include the necessary headers:

```c
#include <zephyr.h>
#include <sys/printk.h>
#include <modem/nrf91.h>
```

Now you can use the nRF9160 driver APIs in your application.

6. Build the project:
Create a build directory and run `cmake` and `ninja` or `make` to build the project:

```sh
$ mkdir build && cd build
$ cmake -GNinja -DBOARD=nrf9160dk_nrf9160 ..
$ ninja
```

7. Flash the project:
Flash the compiled code to your nRF9160 development board:

```sh
$ ninja flash
```

Your project should now be using the nRF Connect SDK nRF9160 driver integrated with the generic Zephyr SDK.

explain composition over inheritance

Composition over inheritance is a design pattern that suggests that code reuse and flexibility can be achieved by composing smaller, more focused objects instead of inheriting from a base or parent class.

Inheritance is a way of creating new classes based on existing classes, where the new class inherits the properties and behaviors of the existing class. While inheritance can be useful, it can lead to tightly coupled, inflexible code, where subclasses become dependent on their parent classes and any changes made to the parent class can potentially affect all subclasses.

On the other hand, composition involves creating small, independent objects and combining them to create more complex objects. This allows for better control over the behavior of objects and can result in more flexible and reusable code.

Composition allows for better separation of concerns and modularity, as each object can be designed and tested independently before being composed into a larger system.

In summary, composition over inheritance promotes a more flexible and adaptable approach to coding by prioritizing the composition of objects over the inheritance of properties and behaviors.

Title: Embracing Real-Time Data Processing with Kafka Streams

Introduction

Welcome to a world of endless possibilities, where data is king and the ability to process it in real-time truly empowers businesses to make sound and efficient decisions. It's no secret that Apache Kafka has become a significant piece in the puzzle of creating and maintaining scalable and reliable data processing systems. In this blog post, we'll delve deeper into the realm of Kafka, focusing on one of its powerful features: Kafka Streams.

What are Kafka Streams?

Kafka Streams is a client library developed for building robust applications and microservices that are capable of processing data in real-time. It offers a simple and powerful programming model, which allows you to perform complex operations such as filtering, mapping, and aggregation with ease.

In a nutshell, Kafka Streams simplifies the development of streaming applications by providing a high-level abstraction over the traditional Kafka producer and consumer APIs. What this essentially means is that one can build an application to process data streams without the need for an external processing cluster.

Kafka Streams has been built with four pillars in mind:

1. High performance
2. Elasticity and scalability
3. Fault tolerance
4. Stateful computations

These elements are essential in ensuring the overall reliability of your data processing system.

Kafka Streams: Getting Started

Working with Kafka Streams begins with the definition of your application's core logic. This logic is essentially a sequence of transformations applied to an input stream. In the world of Kafka Streams, this sequence of transformations is known as a topology.

To get started, you'll need:

- A Kafka cluster for storing and transporting data streams.
- An application which will process those data streams using Kafka Streams APIs.

Apache Kafka provides a quickstart guide, which sets up a local Kafka cluster and showcases how to obtain the Kafka Streams library through Maven or Gradle.

Basic Kafka Streams Concepts

When working with Kafka Streams, it's essential to familiarize yourself with some of the key concepts:

1. Stream: A stream is an ordered sequence of records, where each record represents an event and contains a key, value, and a timestamp.

2. KStream & KTable: KStream and KTable are two primary abstractions within Kafka Streams. A KStream represents an unbounded, continuously updating data stream, whereas a KTable represents a view of the data stream as a changelog containing key-value pairs.

3. Processor API & DSL (Domain Specific Language): Kafka Streams offers two ways to define application logic. The processor API is the lower level abstraction that provides greater flexibility at the cost of more complexity, while the Kafka Streams DSL is a higher level, more concise abstraction for building stream processing applications.

Kafka Streams Example

Let's look at a simple example of a streaming application built using Kafka Streams DSL:

- Objective: Filter records with keys that belong to a certain set and write the filtered records to a new output topic.
- Input: An input Kafka topic containing records in the format (Key, Value).
- Output: An output Kafka topic containing the filtered records.

```java
import org.apache.kafka.streams.StreamsBuilder;
import org.apache.kafka.streams.kstream.KStream;

public class FilterApplication {

   public static void main(String[] args) {
       StreamsBuilder builder = new StreamsBuilder();
       Set<String> keys = Set.of("key1", "key2", "key3");
      
       KStream<String, String> input = builder.stream("input-topic");
       KStream<String, String> filtered = input.filter((key, value) -> keys.contains(key));
      
       filtered.to("output-topic");
   }
}
```

The example showcases a simple Kafka Streams application that filters records based on the keys. It demonstrates the ease with which one can develop a streaming application using Kafka Streams DSL.

Conclusion

Kafka Streams offers simplicity, robustness, and scalability in creating real-time data processing applications. With the ability to scale and handle stateful computations in a fault-tolerant manner, more and more businesses are harnessing the power of Kafka Streams to bring real-time decision-making to their applications. The future of stream processing lies in tools like Kafka Streams, enabling developers to build resilient and feature-rich data processing systems, elevating businesses to new heights.

To achieve load balancing using NGINX in your Kubernetes cluster, follow these steps:

1. Deploy the NGINX Ingress Controller:

In your Kubernetes cluster, deploy the NGINX Ingress Controller using Helm, the package manager for Kubernetes.

First, add the NGINX Ingress repository:

```bash
helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
helm repo update
```

Then, install the ingress-nginx chart:

```bash
helm install my-ingress ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx
```

Wait for the Ingress Controller to be running before you proceed.

2. Create a Load Balancer Service:

Create a load balancer service with the type `LoadBalancer` to expose the NGINX Ingress Controller to the outside world. Create a file called `loadbalancer-service.yaml` with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx-loadbalancer
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx
    app.kubernetes.io/component: controller
  ports:
    - name: http
      protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
    - name: https
      protocol: TCP
      port: 443
      targetPort: https
```

Apply the service to your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f loadbalancer-service.yaml
```

The Load Balancer service will obtain an external IP from your cloud provider. You can monitor the process by running:

```bash
kubectl get svc nginx-loadbalancer
```

Wait until the `EXTERNAL-IP` field is populated.

3. Deploy your Application:

Ensure that your application is running in the cluster with an appropriate deployment and service.

4. Create an Ingress Resource:

An Ingress resource will define the route configurations for your application. Create a file called `my-app-ingress.yaml` with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: my-app-ingress
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "nginx"
spec:
  rules:
  - host: my-app.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: your-app-service
            port:
              number: 80
```

Make sure to replace `my-app.example.com` with your domain name, and replace `your-app-service` with the name of your application's service.

Apply the Ingress resource to your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f my-app-ingress.yaml
```

5. Update your DNS Records:

Update your domain's DNS records to point to the `EXTERNAL-IP` obtained from the Load Balancer service. This will route the traffic to NGINX Ingress Controller, which will, in turn, distribute the traffic to your application instances based on your Ingress configuration.

With the above steps, you've set up NGINX to act as a load balancer in your Kubernetes cluster and distribute traffic evenly among your application instances.
