1. Check if resources are correctly acquired and released:

Ensure that you're properly acquiring and releasing resources, such as image indices, semaphores, and fences. Verify that these resources are not being reused incorrectly, leading to stalls in your renderer.

2. Verify swapchain recreation:

If the window is resized, you may need to recreate the swapchain. Ensure that the swapchain is being recreated when necessary, and during recreation, make sure to wait until the device is idle before destroying and creating new resources.

3. Debugging with RenderDoc:

Use RenderDoc, a graphics debugging tool, to gain insights into your application's behavior during rendering. RenderDoc could help you identify unexpected issues in your rendering pipeline, resource usage, or synchronization.

You can find RenderDoc here: https://renderdoc.org/

4. Check for additional messages from Vulkan Validation Layers:

Make sure you have Vulkan Validation Layers enabled, and check whether there are any messages or warnings reported. Validation layers can help identify incorrect API usage, resource leaks, or synchronization problems that may lead to a stall.

Before running your application, you can also set the `VK_INSTANCE_LAYERS` environment variable to `VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation`. This will enable the validation layers for your application. Ensure that the validation layers are installed on your system; otherwise, your application may fail to launch.

Note: Validation layers may negatively impact performance, so use them only for debugging purposes.

5. Run `vkQueueWaitIdle` before `vkBeginCommandBuffer`:

As a last resort, you can try calling `vkQueueWaitIdle(graphicsQueue)` before you call `vkBeginCommandBuffer(currentCommandBuffer, &beginInfo)`, to ensure the graphics queue is idle before you start recording commands. If this resolves the issue, there might be a deeper synchronization problem in your code that needs further investigation.

Keep in mind that using `vkQueueWaitIdle` may introduce significant performance penalties, and it's not recommended for production code. If it helps fix the stall, it's a temporary solution to help diagnose the problem, but it's important to uncover the real underlying issue.

With these approaches, you should be able to identify the root cause of the hang in the `vkBeginCommandBuffer` call and fix it accordingly.

Ошибка "Cannot resolve symbol '?attr/textColorPrimary'" означает, что атрибут `textColorPrimary` не может быть найден в вашей теме.

Чтобы исправить эту ошибку, вы можете создать свою собственную тему в файле стилей (например, в файле `styles.xml`), которая наследуется от родительской темы `Theme.MaterialComponents.Light` и содержит атрибут `textColorPrimary`. Например, так:

```xml
<style name="MyAppTheme" parent="Theme.MaterialComponents.Light">
    <item name="colorPrimary">@color/my_color_primary</item>
    <item name="colorPrimaryVariant">@color/my_color_primary_variant</item>
    <item name="colorOnPrimary">@color/my_color_on_primary</item>
    <item name="colorSecondary">@color/my_color_secondary</item>
    <item name="colorSecondaryVariant">@color/my_color_secondary_variant</item>
    <item name="colorOnSecondary">@color/my_color_on_secondary</item>
    <item name="textColorPrimary">@color/my_text_color_primary</item>
    <item name="textColorSecondary">@color/my_text_color_secondary</item>
    <!-- и так далее -->
</style>
```

Затем, вы можете установить эту тему для вашего приложения, добавив следующую строку внутри тега `<application>` в файле `AndroidManifest.xml`:

```xml
<application
    android:theme="@style/MyAppTheme">
```

Соответственно, вы должны определить цвета, такие как `my_text_color_primary`, в вашем файле ресурсов `colors.xml`.

```xml
<resources>
    <color name="my_text_color_primary">#000000</color>
    <!-- и так далее -->
</resources>
```

Если вы уже имеете тему, вы можете попробовать добавить атрибут в вашу тему напрямую, например:

```xml
<style name="AppTheme" parent="Theme.MaterialComponents.DayNight">
    <item name="colorPrimary">@color/colorPrimary</item>
    <!-- и так далее -->
    <item name="textColorPrimary">@android:color/white</item>

You have created two descriptor set layouts, but you are only using the sampler descriptor set layout when creating the descriptor set in the Material class. When you create the descriptor set, you should only use the descriptor set layout that has both the uniform buffer and the combined image sampler bindings.

Instead of calling `CreateSamplerDescriptorSetLayout()` function, you should only use the layout returned by the `CreateDescriptorSetLayout()` function.

VkDescriptorSetLayout samplerDescriptorSetLayout = renderer.CreateSamplerDescriptorSetLayout(); // Use this new method to create a separate descriptor layout.

VkDescriptorSetLayout descriptorSetLayout = renderer.CreateDescriptorSetLayout();

squareTile->GetMaterial()->Initialize("C:/shaders/vert_depth2.spv", "C:/shaders/frag_depth2.spv", "C:/textures/texture.jpg", *renderer.GetDevice(), descriptorSetLayout, descriptorSetLayout, descriptorPool, *renderer.GetPhysicalDevice(), *renderer.GetCommandPool(), *renderer.GetGraphicsQueue());

CreateDescriptorSet(samplerDescriptorSetLayout, descriptorPool);

CreateDescriptorSet(descriptorSetLayout, descriptorPool);

1. **Gas estimation error**
   The first error occurs during the gas estimation (eth_estimateGas). The error message - "gas required exceeds allowance (0)" indicates that the available gas is insufficient.

   To resolve this error, instead of estimating the gas, you can simply provide a reasonable gas limit while preparing the transaction. You can adjust the gasLimit value in the `tx` object in the `main()` function:

   ```javascript
   const tx = {
     data: methodParameters.calldata,
     to: methodParameters.address,
     value: methodParameters.value,
     gasLimit: ethers.BigNumber.from('1000000'),  // increase this value accordingly
     gasPrice: await provider.getGasPrice()
   };
   ```

2. **Invalid address error**
   The second error occurs when the code tries to call `SwapRouter.swapCallParameters` method. The error message - "undefined is not a valid address", indicates that the address passed to the function is not valid.

   After looking at the code, it seems that the issue is caused by the SwapRouter instance not being initialized properly. To resolve this error, simply update the `SWAP_ROUTER_ADDRESS`:

   ```javascript
   const SWAP_ROUTER_ADDRESS = '0xE592427A0AEce92De3Edee1F18E0157C05861564';
   ```

After applying the above changes, your code should work as expected. Make sure to test on a testnet before running on the mainnet to avoid losing funds.

$array = [2, 5, 1, 10];

conversation.content: CRTP implementation of a component class to be used for an ecs system

No, this is not a CRTP implementation. The Curiously Recurring Template Pattern involves a class inheriting from another class, which is templated on the derived class itself. 

In this code snippet, you have a `ComponentBase` class, which serves as an interface and does not depend on templates. The `Component` class is templated, but it only derives from `ComponentBase` and does not use the CRTP pattern. The `Component` template class acts like a simple wrapper for classes (defined by the type `C`) that can be managed in a uniform way using the interface provided by `ComponentBase`.

Here's a quick illustration of the difference:

- CRTP: `class Derived : public Base<Derived> {...};`
- Your example: `template <class C> class Component : public ComponentBase {...};`

A CRTP implementation would have the Component inheriting from a template class instantiated with the derived type itself. Your example doesn't exhibit this pattern; instead, it uses inheritance with a non-template base class that provides an interface, and a separate template class that handles different data types.
Which implementation is better?

Choosing between the two implementations depends on your specific use case and requirements.

1. CRTP Implementation:
   - CRTP can generate more efficient code during compilation because the compiler knows the exact derived type at compile-time. This can lead to better inlining and optimization.
   - Using CRTP can make code harder to read and understand, as it involves more advanced template programming concepts.
   - CRTP can be helpful when you want to provide a shared functionality for a family of classes without the overhead of virtual function calls.

2. Non-CRTP Implementation with ComponentBase interface:
   - Using a virtual interface, as shown in your given example, provides a more straightforward way to express the relationship between base and derived classes.
   - The use of virtual functions can introduce runtime overhead, as it requires virtual function calls and, consequently, dynamic dispatch.
   - Using an interface-based approach can make the code more maintainable, as it is easier to comprehend for developers who are not familiar with advanced template programming.

In summary, if performance (especially at compile-time) is a critical concern, and you are comfortable with more advanced template techniques, the CRTP implementation might be a better choice. If ease of understanding and maintainability is more important, the non-CRTP implementation with a virtual interface is likely the better option.

the TrialHandler class in the PsychoPy library can read CSV files and use them as a trial list. The TrialHandler object provides a convenient way to iterate over the trials in the CSV file and access the values of different columns:

from psychopy.data import TrialHandler

# Specify the path to the CSV file
csv_file = 'group_a_stim.csv'

# Create a TrialHandler object with the CSV file as the trialList
trials = TrialHandler(nReps=1, method='random', extraInfo=None, trialList=csv_file, seed=None, name='trials')

# Iterate over the trials and access the values of different columns
for trial in trials:
    # Access values from the CSV columns
    image_file = trial['image']
    condition = trial['condition']
    # Do something with the trial values
    print(f"Image file: {image_file}, Condition: {condition}")



Imagine I have several participants and for each of them I have a row in my csv file with individual stimuli. Can TrialHandler read one row given a participant number?

Yes, you can achieve this by first reading the CSV file to extract the appropriate row for the participant and then passing that row to TrialHandler. Here's an example:

```python
import csv
from psychopy.data import TrialHandler

# Specify the path to the CSV file
csv_file = 'participant_stimuli.csv'

# Read the CSV file as a list of dictionaries
with open(csv_file, mode='r') as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    rows = [row for row in reader]

# Select a participant by their number
participant_number = 3

# Extract the row corresponding to the selected participant
stimuli_row = rows[participant_number - 1]

# Extract the stimuli from the row and format them as a list of dictionaries
stimuli = [
    {'image': stimuli_row['image1'], 'condition': stimuli_row['condition1']},
    {'image': stimuli_row['image2'], 'condition': stimuli_row['condition2']},
    # Add more stimuli if required
]

# Create a TrialHandler object with the stimuli as the trialList
trials = TrialHandler(nReps=1, method='random', extraInfo=None, trialList=stimuli, seed=None, name='trials')

# Iterate over the trials and access the values of different columns
for trial in trials:
    # Access values from the CSV columns
    image_file = trial['image']
    condition = trial['condition']
    # Do something with the trial values
    print(f"Image file: {image_file}, Condition: {condition}")
```

This code snippet assumes you have a CSV file with columns named `image1`, `condition1`, `image2`, `condition2`, and so on, but you can adjust the code to match your CSV file's structure.

In FiveM, you can use object-oriented programming with the help of the Lua OOP library "middleclass". To spawn a vehicle with a registered command, you can follow this example:

First, make sure to download and include middleclass in your script:
https://github.com/kikito/middleclass

Next, create a class for spawning vehicles:

```lua
local class = require('middleclass')

local VehicleSpawner = class('VehicleSpawner')

function VehicleSpawner:initialize(vehicleModel)
  self.vehicleModel = vehicleModel
end

function VehicleSpawner:spawnVehicle(x, y, z, heading)
  local modelHash = GetHashKey(self.vehicleModel)
  RequestModel(modelHash)

  while not HasModelLoaded(modelHash) do
    Wait(0) -- Wait for the mode to load
  end

  local vehicle = CreateVehicle(modelHash, x, y, z, heading, true, false)

  return vehicle
end

return VehicleSpawner
```

Now, in your main script, you can use the VehicleSpawner class to spawn a vehicle when a command is registered:

```lua
local VehicleSpawner = require('VehicleSpawner')

-- Register the command
RegisterCommand('spawnvehicle', function(source, args)
    -- Ensure the player input a vehicle model name
    if #args < 1 then
        TriggerEvent('chat:addMessage', {
                color = {255, 0, 0},
                multiline = true,
                args = {"Error", "Please specify a vehicle model"}
        })
        return
    end

    -- Get the vehicle model name
    local vehicleModel = args[1]

    -- Create a VehicleSpawner instance
    local spawner = VehicleSpawner:new(vehicleModel)

    -- Get player ped
    local playerPed = PlayerPedId()

    -- Get player's current position and heading
    local x, y, z = table.unpack(GetEntityCoords(playerPed))
    local heading = GetEntityHeading(playerPed)

    -- Spawn the vehicle
    local spawnedVehicle = spawner:spawnVehicle(x, y, z + 1, heading)

    -- Set the player as the vehicle's driver
    TaskWarpPedIntoVehicle(playerPed, spawnedVehicle, -1)

    -- Output a message in the chat
    TriggerEvent('chat:addMessage', {
            color = {0, 255, 0},
            multiline = true,
            args = {"Success", "Vehicle spawned: " .. vehicleModel}
    })

end, false) -- false means this command is available to everyone
```

With this example, when a player types `/spawnvehicle [vehicleModel]`, a new vehicle will be spawned at their location.

1. Custom build system:
The most efficient solution is to create a custom build system in Sublime Text to redirect the build output to a file and a separate window:

- Go to Tools > Build System > New Build System.
- Copy and paste the following JSON content:

```json
{
  "shell_cmd": "rustc $file --out-dir $file_path > $file_path/result.txt 2>&1",
  "selector": "source.rust"
}
```

- Save the build system file as `rustc_custom.sublime-build`.
- Select the custom build system from Tools > Build System > rustc_custom.
- Now when you build a Rust file (`CTRL + B`), the build results are output to a `result.txt` file in the same directory as the Rust source file.

2. Custom build script:
Wrap the Rust build command in a shell script and call that script instead:

- Create a shell script called `build_rust.sh`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
rustc $1 --out-dir $(dirname $1) > $(dirname $1)/result.txt 2>&1
```

- Make it executable: `chmod +x build_rust.sh`.
- Update the custom build system in Sublime Text to call this script:

```json
{
  "shell_cmd": "/path/to/build_rust.sh $file",
  "selector": "source.rust"
}
```

3. Python build script:
Create a Python script that builds the Rust project, captures the output, and saves it to a file:

- Create a Python script called `build_rust.py`:

```python
import sys
import os
import subprocess

source_file = sys.argv[1]
build_dir = os.path.dirname(source_file)

result = subprocess.run(["rustc", source_file, "--out-dir", build_dir], capture_output=True, text=True)
with open(os.path.join(build_dir, "result.txt"), "w") as f:
    f.write(result.stdout + result.stderr)
```

- Update the custom build system in Sublime Text to call this Python script:

```json
{
  "shell_cmd": "python3 /path/to/build_rust.py $file",
  "selector": "source.rust"
}
```

4. Custom build script with separate window output:

```bash

echo "-----Rust Build Results-----" > /path/to/separate_window/sublime_rust_result.txt
cat $(dirname $1)/result.txt >> /path/to/separate_window/sublime_rust_result.txt
```

- This will create a new file in a separate directory containing the build results, which you can open in a new Sublime Text window.

        .args(&["--out-dir", "target"])
        .output()
        .expect("failed to execute rustc");

    std::fs::write("result.txt", &output.stdout).expect("Unable to write to result.txt");
    std::fs::write("result_stderr.txt", &output.stderr).expect("Unable to write to result_stderr.txt");

You can use the following command to filter the logs based on the application's package name and log level:

```
adb logcat -v time -s <PACKAGE_NAME>:<LOG_LEVEL>
```

Replace `<PACKAGE_NAME>` with the package name of the application you want to filter by, and `<LOG_LEVEL>` with the log level you want to filter by (e.g. VERBOSE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR).

For example, to view only DEBUG level logs for the "com.example.myapp" package, you can use the following command:

If you want to save the filtered logs to a file, add the following to the command:

> <FILENAME>.txt

Replace `<FILENAME>` with the name of the file you want to save the logs to. For example:

```

conversation.content: How to add 3rd party headers and code into a professional visual studio personal project?

To add a third-party library or headers in a professional Visual Studio project, you would typically follow these steps:

**Step 1: Download the third-party library**

Download the library you want to use in your project. If it's a header-only library, you'll only need the header files. If it has source code, you'll need the source files (*.cpp, *.c), as well. You may also need to download pre-compiled binaries or build the library from source if required.

**Step 2: Add the header files to your project**

1. Create a folder, e.g., `external` or `libraries`, inside your project directory to keep third-party headers and source files.
2. Copy the header files of the third-party library into the newly created folder.
3. In Visual Studio, right-click on your project in the Solution Explorer, then select "Add" and choose "Existing Item".
4. Browse to the folder where you added the header files, select them, and click "Add".

**Step 3: Add the library to your include path**

1. In Visual Studio, right-click on your project in the Solution Explorer and choose "Properties".
2. Navigate to "Configuration Properties" > "C/C++" > "General".
3. In the "Additional Include Directories" field, add the path to the folder containing the third-party header files. For example, if your project is in `C:\MyProject` and you created a `libraries` folder with the header files, add `C:\MyProject\libraries`.

**Step 4: Include the source files or link against the library binaries (if required)**

*If the third-party library is header-only, you can skip this step.*

For libraries with source files:

1. Add the source files (*.cpp, *.c) to the folder you created in step 2.
2. In Visual Studio, right-click on your project in Solution Explorer, select "Add", then "Existing Item".
3. Browse to the folder containing the source files, select them, and click "Add".

For libraries with pre-compiled binaries:

1. Place the library binaries (*.lib, *.dll) in a folder, like `C:\MyProject\libraries`.
2. In your project's properties, navigate to "Configuration Properties" > "Linker" > "General".
3. In "Additional Library Directories", add the path to the folder containing the library binaries.
4. Go to "Configuration Properties" > "Linker" > "Input" and add the *.lib files to the "Additional Dependencies" field.

**Step 5: Include the headers in your source code**

Now you can include the third-party headers in your source code using the `#include` directive, like you would for any other header:

```cpp
#include "third_party_library_header.h" // Replace this with the correct header file name

// ... Your code ...
```

That's it! You've added a third-party library to your professional Visual Studio personal project. Remember to rebuild your project after making these changes.

Additionally, if you use third-party libraries, make sure to comply with their licenses and acknowledge the authors as required.

5. Depending on your game or application's requirements, you may need to include conditions in your scripts to check whether the character is controlled by a player or an AI agent. This can be done, for example, by storing information on the control mode, and checking it before executing certain actions or responding to certain inputs.

6. In the Unity Editor, add both the PlayerController component and the MyAgent component to your character's GameObject. The character should now be able to be controlled by either the player or the ML Agent, depending on the setup and conditions you defined in your scripts.

In Unity's ML Agents, you typically create a new script called "AgentScript" that inherits from the "Agent" class provided by the ML-Agents API. You don't have to modify your existing PlayerController script.

Here are the steps to create an agent:

1. Create a new script called "AgentScript" and open it in the editor.
2. Replace the "MonoBehaviour" class inheritance with the "Agent" class provided by ML-Agents.
3. Override the necessary methods which are used to define agent behavior:

    - `OnEpisodeBegin()`: Called when an episode begins. Reset the environment and agent to their initial state.
    - `CollectObservations(VectorSensor sensor)`: Provide the agent with the necessary observations (e.g., environment state) to make decisions.
    - `OnActionReceived(float[] vectorAction)`: Called when the agent receives an action. Execute the action and provide a reward or punishment based on the agent's action.
    - `Heuristic(float[] actionsOut)`: Write any manual control of the agent in this method. It can be helpful in testing your agent before training.

4. Attach your AgentScript to the appropriate game object which will be your agent in the Unity Editor.

Instead of modifying your existing PlayerController script, you will use the AgentScript to control the agent. You can leave the PlayerController script for manual control and debugging purposes, and make use of the Heuristic function in the AgentScript during these situations, as it allows manual control of the agent.

You need to make references to other game objects or scripts in your AgentScript if they are needed to make decisions. But you don't need to make references to the AgentScript in your PlayerController script or any other script, since the agent will be controlled by the ML-Agents algorithms, not by the user input.

Note that while training the agent, you should disable the PlayerController script to avoid interference with the training process.

conversation.content: in unity's ML Agents do I need to modify my PlayerController which works with player input? or do I need to create a new script and make references in the code to each other?

In Unity's ML Agents, you typically don't modify your existing PlayerController script directly. Instead, you create a new script that inherits from the Agent class. This new script will control the agent's interaction with the environment, receive observations, and execute actions determined by the trained model.

You can reuse some code from your PlayerController in this new agent script if it's related to agent's movement, decision-making, etc. However, player input-related code should be separated as it doesn't apply to the agent.

Here's a high-level overview of the steps you need to follow:

1. Create a new C# script that inherits from the Agent class (from "using Unity.MLAgents;") and attach it to your game object that you want to train.

2. Implement the required methods such as `OnEpisodeBegin()`, `CollectObservations()`, and `OnActionReceived()`. These methods are responsible for resetting the environment, collecting input observations for training, and executing the necessary actions based on the output of the trained model.

3. If needed, you can keep your PlayerController script for player control during testing and development. However, make sure that the new agent script and PlayerController script do not interfere with each other. You may use conditional checks like "#if UNITY_EDITOR" in your PlayerController script to disable certain sections of the code when the build is running in the Unity Editor to avoid conflicts.

4. In your new agent script, you can reference and utilize any necessary components or functionality from your PlayerController script. This allows you to use the same logic for movement or other actions, reducing code duplication. However, you may need to make some adjustments to ensure compatibility with the Agent class.

5. After implementing the new agent script, set up your ML-Agent training environment following Unity's ML-Agents documentation, create your training configuration file, and start training your agent using the ML-Agents Python package.

Remember that your new agent script should focus on agent logic rather than player input. When you want to test your trained agent, simply enable the new agent script and disable the PlayerController script, so that the agent acts based on the trained model instead of player input.

Here is one approach to remove duplicate entries in a dictionary based on the value (assuming the value is a list):

```python
def remove_duplicates(dictionary):
    """
    Removes duplicates from dictionary based on the value (which is a list).
    """
    values = list(dictionary.values())
    for k, v in dictionary.items():
        # Check if any other value contains all of the elements in the current value
        if any(set(v).issubset(set(other_v)) for other_v in values if other_v != v):
            # If so, remove the current key/value pair from the dictionary
            del dictionary[k]
    return dictionary
```

Here's an example usage:

```python
>>> d = {'a': [1, 2, 3], 'b': [2, 3], 'c': [4, 5], 'd': [1, 2, 3, 4]}
>>> remove_duplicates(d)
{'c': [4, 5], 'd': [1, 2, 3, 4]}
```

In this example, the 'a' and 'b' keys are considered duplicates because the values [1, 2, 3] and [2, 3] are both subsets of [1, 2, 3, 4], which is the value of the 'd' key. Therefore, those keys are removed from the dictionary, leaving only the 'c' and 'd' keys with their values.

A common logging practice for Java Spring Boot microservices system is to use a centralized logging system. Some popular logging frameworks that are commonly used with Spring Boot are:

1. Logback - a mature, reliable and fast logging framework that is widely used and supported by the Spring Boot community.

2. Log4j2 - a fast and flexible logging framework that provides powerful configuration options and supports custom log format.

3. Java Util Logging (JUL) - a standard logging framework implemented in the Java Development Kit (JDK), which provides basic logging capabilities but lacks the advanced features of Logback and Log4j2.

Using a centralized logging system allows you to aggregate logs from all your microservices in one place, making it easier to monitor and analyze system performance. Some popular centralized logging solutions for Spring Boot microservices are:

1. Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana (ELK) - a powerful open-source logging stack with great search and visualization capabilities.

2. Graylog - an open-source log management platform that provides full-text search, alerting, and centralized management features.

3. Splunk - a commercial logging solution that provides powerful search and analysis capabilities, as well as real-time monitoring and alerting features.

By configuring your microservices to send their logs to a centralized system, you can easily monitor and troubleshoot issues across your entire system.

Make a Multi-Dimensional Array in java that can hold two numbers each as map coordinates and the ability to add more map coordinates

To create a multi-dimensional array in Java that can hold two numbers each as map coordinates and the ability to add more map coordinates, follow these steps:

1. Declare a variable to represent the multi-dimensional array. For example:

```java
int[][] mapCoordinates;
```

2. Initialize the multi-dimensional array with an initial size. For example:

```java
mapCoordinates = new int[5][2];
```

This creates a multi-dimensional array with 5 rows and 2 columns to hold x and y coordinates.

3. Add map coordinates to the multi-dimensional array. For example:

```java
mapCoordinates[0][0] = 1; // x coordinate of first map location
mapCoordinates[0][1] = 2; // y coordinate of first map location
mapCoordinates[1][0] = 4; // x coordinate of second map location
mapCoordinates[1][1] = 5; // y coordinate of second map location
// add more map coordinates as needed
```

4. To add more map coordinates to the multi-dimensional array, you can resize the array and copy the existing map coordinates to the new array. For example:

```java
int[][] newMapCoordinates = new int[10][2]; // create larger array
for (int i = 0; i < mapCoordinates.length; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < mapCoordinates[i].length; j++) {
        newMapCoordinates[i][j] = mapCoordinates[i][j]; // copy existing map coordinates to new array
    }
}
```

5. Once the new array has been created and filled with existing map coordinates, you can add new map coordinates as before:

```java
newMapCoordinates[5][0] = 10; // x coordinate of new map location
newMapCoordinates[5][1] = 12; // y coordinate of new map location
// add more map coordinates as needed
```

Overall, creating a multi-dimensional array in Java to hold map coordinates is similar to creating any other type of multi-dimensional array. The key is to properly initialize the array and then use nested for loops to access and manipulate its elements. By resizing the array and copying the existing elements to the new array, you can add more map coordinates as needed.

Kotlin does not have a built-in function to break out of a lambda (like a `return` statement in a loop). However, you can achieve the desired outcome using different means depending on your use case. Here are a couple of ways to do this:

1. If you want to stop filtering after a certain condition is met, you can use the `takeWhile` function:

```kotlin
val list = listOf(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
val filteredList = list.takeWhile { it < 4 } // results in listOf(1, 2, 3)
```

2. If you want to break out of a lambda inside forEach or other scenarios, you can use the `forEach` function with labels:

```kotlin
val list = listOf(1, 2, 3, 1000, 4, 5)

val newList = mutableListOf<Int>()
run loop@{
    list.forEach { item ->
        if(item == 1000)
            return@loop // break
        newList.add(item)
    }
}
```

Keep in mind that breaking the flow is not idiomatic in functional programming, so consider restructuring your code using other higher-order functions like `map`, `filter`, and `fold` if needed.

conversation.content: как и где создавать dimens.xml:

Файл dimens.xml создается в папке res/values. Если данной папки не существует, ее можно создать вручную. 

Для создания файла dimens.xml нужно выполнить следующие шаги: 

1. Откройте папку res в своем проекте Android Studio.

2. Нажмите правой кнопкой мыши на папке values и выберите пункт New -> Values resource file.

3. В окне Create new XML resource введите имя файла dimens.

4. Выберите тип ресурса dimen (значения размеров).

5. Нажмите кнопку OK.

Теперь вы можете открыть файл dimens.xml и добавить значения размеров, которые используются в вашем приложении. 

Например: 

```xml
<resources>
    <dimen name="text_size_small">12sp</dimen>
    <dimen name="text_size_medium">16sp</dimen>
    <dimen name="text_size_large">24sp</dimen>
</resources>
```

Это пример файла dimens.xml, который содержит три значения размеров текста (12sp, 16sp и 24sp) с именами text_size_small, text_size_medium и text_size_large соответственно. 

Вы можете использовать эти значения в своем коде, обращаясь к ним через метод getResources().getDimension(). 

Например: 

```java
float smallTextSize = getResources().getDimension(R.dimen.text_size_small);
textView.setTextSize(smallTextSize);
``` 

В этом примере тексту в TextView будет установлен размер, равный значению text_size_small из файла dimens.xml.

conversation.content: 现在有两个springboot项目，分别为A和B。A项目主要存放公用的工具类、常量类、枚举类、http请求工具类等，A项目没有启动类。B项目为主项目，负责为前端查询并输出数据，现在我将A项目引入到B项目。当B项目启动时，报错提示A项目中的某一个加了@Component注解的类中的@Value注解没有获取到配置文件中的数据，请问该怎么解决
现在有两个springboot项目，分别为A和B。A项目主要存放公用的工具类、常量类、枚举类、http请求工具类等，A项目没有启动类。B项目为主项目，负责为前端查询并输出数据，现在我将A项目引入到B项目。当B项目启动时，报错提示A项目中的某一个加了@Component注解的类中的@Value注解没有获取到配置文件中的数据（A需要读取B中的配置文件数据），请问该怎么解决

解决此问题，需要在 A 项目中读取 B 项目中的配置文件信息。可以通过以下两种方式实现：

1. 在 A 项目中使用 `@PropertySource` 和 `@Value` 注解读取 B 项目的配置文件

在 A 项目中使用 `@PropertySource` 和 `@Value` 注解，读取 B 项目中的配置文件内容，如下所示：

```java
@Configuration
@PropertySource(value = "classpath:application.properties")
public class AppConfig {
    @Value("${spring.datasource.url}")
    private String dataSourceUrl;
    @Value("${spring.datasource.username}")
    private String dataSourceUsername;
    @Value("${spring.datasource.password}")
    private String dataSourcePassword;
    //...
}
```

这样在 A 项目中就能够读取到 B 项目中配置信息，然后在 A 项目中的工具类、常量类、枚举类、http请求工具类等等中使用这些配置。

2. 通过将 B 项目的配置文件打包进 A 项目中的 jar 包进行读取

在 B 项目中的 `pom.xml` 文件中添加 Maven 插件用于将配置文件打包至 jar 包内，如下所示：

```xml
<build>
    <resources>
        <resource>
            <directory>src/main/resources</directory>
            <includes>
                <include>application.properties</include>
            </includes>
        </resource>
    </resources>

    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-resources-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>3.2.0</version>
            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <id>copy-resources</id>
                    <phase>process-resources</phase>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>copy-resources</goal>
                    </goals>
                    <configuration>
                        <outputDirectory>${basedir}/target/classes</outputDirectory>
                        <resources>
                            <resource>
                                <directory>src/main/resources</directory>
                                <includes>
                                    <include>application.properties</include>
                                </includes>
                            </resource>
                        </resources>
                    </configuration>
                </execution>
            </executions>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>
```

然后在 A 项目中直接读取 jar 包中的配置文件，如下所示：

```java
Properties properties = new Properties();
properties.load(getClass().getResourceAsStream("/application.properties"));
String dataSourceUrl = properties.getProperty("spring.datasource.url");
String dataSourceUsername = properties.getProperty("spring.datasource.username");
String dataSourcePassword = properties.getProperty("spring.datasource.password");
//...
```

这样就可以在 A 项目中直接读取 B 项目中的配置文件信息了。

conversation.content: undefined reference to `va_start'

This error message usually occurs during compilation and indicates that the compiler cannot find the definition of the function va_start. 

The function va_start is from the C standard library and is used for variable argument lists. It needs to be included in the source code using the following header file:

```c
#include <stdarg.h>
```

To solve this error, make sure that the header file is included and that the C standard library is linked during compilation. This can be done by including the following flag during compilation:

```bash
-lc
```

If the error still persists, check if the compiler supports C99 or later, as va_start is part of the C99 standard and later versions.

in C# HttpClient's SendAsync method is not getting called, but the inner handler is,
how to intercept the innerhandler's SendAsync method?

How DelegatingHandler works in C#?

so if the top handler has a timeout of 20 seconds, and it's inner-handler has a timeout of 10 seconds,
Which timeout is used?

`DelegatingHandler` is an implementation of `HttpMessageHandler` in C# that acts as a middleman between two other `HttpMessageHandler` instances. Its primary purpose is to intercept and modify requests and responses between the caller (e.g. `HttpClient`) and the actual handler responsible for sending the request (e.g. `HttpClientHandler`). You can think of a `DelegatingHandler` as a wrapper around another `HttpMessageHandler`.

When you use a `DelegatingHandler`, the `SendAsync` method can be overridden to modify the request before it's passed to the inner handler, and to modify the response before it's returned to the caller.

The `HttpClient` uses the `DelegatingHandler` chain to execute requests. The order of handlers is important, as it determines the sequence in which they are called when executing a request. The top handler in the chain will call its inner handler, which will call its inner handler, and so on.

Regarding your question about timeouts, the timeout of the top handler (`HttpClient`) is the one that gets used. The inner handler's timeout will not be considered. If a request takes more than 20 seconds to execute, a `TaskCanceledException` (wrapping a `TimeoutException`) will be thrown.

However, the inner handler may have its own logic for handling timeouts which may be independent of the `HttpClient`'s timeout, but that will depend on the actual implementation. For example, the request might be subject to a lower timeout (e.g., DNS resolution or TCP connection) within the inner handler that is not visible to `HttpClient`. But ultimately, the outer handler's (i.e., `HttpClient`) timeout will be the one that matters for the entire request's duration.

In order to register your multi connectors microservice to the Eureka server, you need to ensure that you have correctly configured your microservice.

Here's a checklist to help you troubleshoot the problem:

1. Make sure you added the correct dependencies in the `pom.xml` or `build.gradle` file:

- For Maven (`pom.xml`):

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-netflix-eureka-client</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

- For Gradle (`build.gradle`):

```gradle
implementation 'org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-starter-netflix-eureka-client'
```

2. Ensure you have enabled Eureka client configurations in your microservice `application.properties` or `application.yml` file:

- For `application.properties`:

```properties
spring.application.name=my-microservice
eureka.client.service-url.defaultZone=http://localhost:8761/eureka/
spring.cloud.discovery.enabled=true
```

- For `application.yml`:

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: my-microservice
eureka:
  client:
    service-url:
      defaultZone: http://localhost:8761/eureka/
spring:
  cloud:
    discovery:
      enabled: true
```

3. Add the `@EnableEurekaClient` annotation to the main class of your microservice:

```java
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.cloud.netflix.eureka.EnableEurekaClient;

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableEurekaClient
public class MyMicroserviceApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(MyMicroserviceApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

4. Restart your Eureka server and your microservice applications.

5. Check the Eureka dashboard at `http://localhost:8761/` to see if your microservice is registered.

If your microservice still doesn't appear in the Eureka dashboard, try checking the logs for any error messages or warnings, and make sure that the Eureka server and microservice instances are running on the correct ports and addresses.

Your implementation looks good and thread-safe. Here are some suggestions to improve it:

1. Use ConcurrentDictionary instead of Dictionary

ConcurrentDictionary is a thread-safe dictionary provided by .NET Framework and does not allow multiple threads to modify the dictionary at the same time. It provides better performance than locking the entire dictionary and also avoids deadlocks.

2. Use DateTimeOffset.UtcNow instead of DateTimeOffset.Now

When dealing with time in a distributed system, it is better to use UTC time rather than local time. It reduces the chance of timezone-related issues and makes it easier to compare time across different systems.

3. Use tasks instead of threads

When dealing with asynchronous operations, it is better to use tasks instead of threads. Tasks provide a higher level of abstraction and are easier to manage than threads.

4. Use CancellationToken to cancel the background task

If you want to stop the background task that removes the expired items from the cache, you can use CancellationToken to cancel it. It is safer than using the Thread.Abort method.

5. Implement IDisposable interface to dispose the resources

You can implement the IDisposable interface and dispose the resources such as the background task and the CancellationTokenSource when the object is no longer needed. It ensures that the resources are released properly and avoids memory leaks.

6. Use a configurable number of background tasks

If you have a large number of items in the cache and it takes a long time to remove the expired items, you can divide the cache into multiple partitions and run a background task for each partition. It improves the performance and reduces the chance of deadlocks.

y in Node.js. It provides several methods and properties to manipulate file paths.

Some of the commonly used methods are:

- path.join(): Joins all given path segments together, using the platform-specific separator (/ or \).
- path.resolve(): Resolves a sequence of paths or path segments into an absolute path.
- path.parse(): Returns an object with the components of a path (dir, root, base, ext, name).
- path.basename(): Returns the last portion of a path (file name) or removes the file extension.
- path.dirname(): Returns the directory name of a path.

For example, to join two path segments together, we can use:

```javascript
const path = require('path');

const myPath = path.join('/my', 'path');
console.log(myPath); // output: /my/path
```

Or to get the directory name of a path:

```javascript
const path = require('path');

const filePath = '/my/path/file.txt';
const dirName = path.dirname(filePath);
console.log(dirName); // output: /my/path
```

Path manipulation and parsing is a very common task in Node.js applications, and the "path" module makes it very easy to do so.
Cannot access "path.join" in client code

You cannot access "path.join" directly in client-side code because the "path" module is part of the Node.js environment and not available in the browser.

However, there are alternatives that you can use to manipulate file paths in the client-side code. One solution is to use a third-party library such as "path-browserify" or "path-umd" that provides a browser-compatible implementation of the "path" module.

To use "path-browserify", you can install it from npm:

```
npm install path-browserify
```

Then, you can import it in your client-side code and use "path.join" like this:

```javascript
const path = require('path-browserify');

const myPath = path.join('/my', 'path');
console.log(myPath); // output: /my/path
```

Alternatively, you can use the "url" API available in the browser to manipulate URLs:

```javascript
const path = '/my/path';
const filename = 'file.txt';
const newPath = new URL(filename, `https://www.example.com${path}`).pathname;
console.log(newPath); // output: /my/path/file.txt
```

Keep in mind that these solutions may have limitations and differences compared to the Node.js implementation of "path". Make sure to review the documentation and consider if it fits your requirements.

To make an actor move with a moving platform in Unreal Engine 4, you can use the following steps:

1. First, make sure that both the actor and the moving platform have their movement components attached to them (if not already).

2. In the Blueprint editor for your actor, create a new "Tick" event or use the existing one provided by default.

3. In the "Event Tick" graph, get a reference to your moving platform. You can either use a direct hard reference (if the platform is part of the same blueprint) or use a "Get All Actors of Class" node with the class of your moving platform and select the first one from the array (if the platform is in a separate blueprint).

4. Use the "Get Actor Location" node to get the position of both the platform and the actor.

5. Create a "Vector + Vector" node and add the location of the platform to the location of the actor.

6. Use a "Set Actor Location" node to update the actor's position based on the result from step 5.

7. The actor should now move along with the platform while still being able to move independently. You might want to add some collision checks to make sure the actor actually stands on the platform, or use a "Get Overlapping Actors" node to check if the actor is overlapping with the platform.

Here's some sample blueprint script for reference:

```
Event Tick
  |
  Get All Actors of Class -> (Your platform class)
  |                |
  Get(0)          Get Actor Location (Platform Location)
  |
Get Actor Location (Actor Location)
  |
Vector + Vector (Actor Location + Platform Location)
  |
Set Actor Location
```

With this setup, the actor should move along with the platform, while still being able to move by itself using its movement inputs and logic.

This issue can be caused by an unstable training, large learning rates, very large rewards, or numerical issues related to observations.

Here are some suggestions to address this problem:

1. **Normalize Observations**: If the collected observations are not normalized, they might cause instability in the training process. Enable observation normalization in your YAML configuration file:

```
network_settings:
  normalize: true
```

2. **Decrease Learning Rate**: A large learning rate might result in unstable training. Try lowering the learning rate in your YAML configuration file:

```
hyperparameters:
  learning_rate: 0.0001
```

3. **Adjust Rewards**: If the rewards given to the agent are very large (e.g., high positive or high negative values), this might create an issue in the calculations. Ensure that the rewards returned to your agents are reasonably sized (close to -1, 0, or 1) and not overly large.

4. **Clamp Action Values**: To deal with NaN values in actions, you can try clamping the continuous actions using "tanh" activation function after computing the actions:

    - `Detectable Tags`: A list of GameObject tags that the sensor can detect. Make sure the objects you want to detect have these tags assigned.
    - `Transform`: A reference to the agent's Transform component (automatically assigned when you add the component).

The Ray Perception Sensor 2D component in ML-Agents allows your agents to perceive their environment using raycast sensors, which are handy for detecting objects in 2D environments. Raycasting is a form of perception that allows an agent to "see" objects using rays, casted from a certain direction or directions in a specified range.

To use the Ray Perception Sensor 2D component in your ML-Agent, follow these steps:

Step 1: Add the Ray Perception Sensor 2D
1. Select your agent GameObject in Unity.
2. In the Inspector, click "Add Component".
3. Search for "Ray Perception Sensor 2D" and add it to the Agent GameObject.

Step 2: Configure the Ray Perception Sensor 2D
1. In the Ray Perception Sensor 2D component within the Inspector, set the number of rays and the ray angle.
2. Define the observation's maximum range by setting the Ray Length.
3. Add the tags of the detectable GameObjects (such as "Wall", "Food", etc.) to the Detectable Tags list.

Step 3: Add Observations in the Agent Script
1. In your PlayerController script, add the RayPerceptionSensorComponent2D namespace at the top:
```csharp
using Unity.MLAgents.Sensors;
```
2. In the CollectObservations method, you no longer need to call GetComponentsInChildren since the Ray Perception Sensor gathers observations automatically. To access the Ray Perception Sensor component in your script, you need to get the component:
```csharp
RayPerceptionSensorComponent2D rayPerception = GetComponent<RayPerceptionSensorComponent2D>();
```
Step 4: Train Your Agent
Now, you can train your agent, and it will use the Ray Perception Sensor 2D for its observations.

Both RayPerceptionSensorComponent2D and RayPerceptionSensorComponent3D automatically add their observations when you use the PlayerController script, removing the need to manually gather data within the CollectObservations function. The steps described above will integrate the Ray Perception Sensor 2D component so your agent can use 2D raycasting for object detection.

Remember that raycasting works by detecting objects within the ray's trajectory. If an object is behind another object, the agent will not be able to perceive it as the ray will stop at the first object it hits. Following this approach, your agent will more accurately perceive the world like a real-world agent, allowing them to learn to better navigate their environment.

In order to send requests from different IP addresses when using Tor, you need to change the Tor circuit. However, Tor doesn't have a built-in function for changing circuits per request. Instead, you can use a function from the Stem library that sends a new circuit signal to the Tor control port. This solution does not guarantee a new IP address for each request, but it increases the likelihood.

Here's an updated Python script that achieves your requirement:

```python
import time
import requests
from stem import Signal
from stem.control import Controller

proxies = {
    'http': 'socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050',
    'https': 'socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050'
}

url = 'http://ip-api.com/json/'  # A website that returns information about the connecting IP address

# Function to send a new circuit signal
def change_tor_circuit():
    with Controller.from_port(port=9051) as controller: # Default Tor control port
        controller.authenticate()                       # Authentificate with control port
        controller.signal(Signal.NEWNYM)               # Send new circuit signal

# Function to send a request using the Tor proxy
def send_request(url):
    response = requests.get(url, proxies=proxies)
    return response.json()

# Main loop to send requests, one request per second
for i in range(5):  # Number of requests you want to send, change this to your desired value
    ip_info = send_request(url)
    print(f"Request {i+1}: IP address: {ip_info['query']}, Country: {ip_info['country']}")
    
    change_tor_circuit()  # Change circuit after each request
    time.sleep(1)  # Wait 1 second before sending the next request
```

   ```
   pip install stem
   ```

2. Open your Tor configuration file, usually called `torrc`, and edit it as follows:

To register a command with arguments in Lua for FiveM scripting server-side, you can use the `RegisterCommand` function provided by FiveM. Here is an example code snippet:

```lua
RegisterCommand('mycmd', function(source, args, rawCommand)
  -- Code to execute when the command is called
  -- The argument values are stored in the `args` table
  print('Command executed with arguments:')
  for i = 1, #args do
    print('  ['..i..']: '..args[i])
  end
end, false)
```

In this example, the command is registered with the name `'mycmd'` and a callback function that takes three arguments:

- `source`: the ID of the player who triggered the command (or `0` if it was executed from the console)
- `args`: a table containing the arguments passed to the command (split by spaces)
- `rawCommand`: the full text of the command, including the command name and arguments

The `false` parameter at the end of the `RegisterCommand` call specifies that the command is not restricted to administrators. If you want to limit the command to certain players or groups, you can specify a permission string instead (e.g. `'admin'`).

To execute this command in-game, you can type `/mycmd arg1 arg2 arg3` in the chat or console (replacing `arg1`, `arg2`, and `arg3` with your desired argument values).

registercommand server side fivem lua 
clients can trigger it. how do i stop them from doing so?

One way to prevent clients from triggering a server-side command is to include an authorization check within the command script. This can be achieved by checking the source of the command (i.e. the player) and ensuring that they have the required permissions or authorization to execute the command.

For example, you could include a check for the player's identifier (a unique identifier assigned by the server) and compare it against a list of authorized players or user groups.

If the command is triggered by an unauthorized player, you can simply return a message indicating that they are not authorized to execute the command.

Here is an example of how you can include an authorization check within your server-side command script:

```lua
RegisterCommand("mycommand", function(source, args, rawCommand)
   local playerIdentifier = GetPlayerIdentifier(source, 0)

   -- Check if the player is authorized to execute the command
   if not IsPlayerAuthorized(playerIdentifier) then
      TriggerClientEvent("chatMessage", source, "^1Error: You are not authorized to execute this command")
      return
   end

   -- Your command logic goes here
   -- ...

end, false)
```

In this example, `IsPlayerAuthorized()` is a function that checks whether the player with the given `playerIdentifier` is authorized to execute the command. You can define this function however you like, depending on how you want to handle authorization.

To prevent clients from triggering a server-side command in FiveM, you can use the 'TriggerServerEvent' function only for authorized sources. This way, it allows you to control who is allowed to perform certain actions on the server side. Here's an example of how you can implement such restriction:

1. Create a new file named `restrict_server_command.lua` in your FiveM resource folder.
2. Add the following code to `restrict_server_command.lua`:

```lua
-- Server Side
RegisterNetEvent('my_server_command')
AddEventHandler('my_server_command', function(param1, param2, ...)

    -- Validate the source
    if not IsValidSource(source) then
        print('Unauthorized attempt to trigger server command from: ' .. source)
        return
    end

    -- Your command logic goes here after you validated the source client
    -- ...

end)

-- Method to check if the source is valid/authorized
function IsValidSource(source)
    -- Add your logic here to validate the source, e.g., checking for specific player identifier, permission, etc.
    -- For example, it could look like this:

    local xPlayer = ESX.GetPlayerFromId(source)

    if xPlayer and (xPlayer.getGroup() == "admin" or xPlayer.getGroup() == "superadmin") then
        return true
    else
        return false
    end
end
```

3. Replace `'my_server_command'` with your desired event name.
4. Replace `IsValidSource` function with your own logic to check if the source is authorized. In this example, we are using the popular ESX framework and checking if the player's group is either "admin" or "superadmin".
5. On the client-side, use `TriggerServerEvent` to call the server-side event. Make sure you're using the same event name as in the server-side code:

```lua
TriggerServerEvent('my_server_command', param1, param2, ...)
```

This way, clients will still be able to trigger the server-side event, but any unauthorized attempt will be blocked, logged, and ignored by the server.

To display images in a RecyclerView in Kotlin, you can use the following steps:

1. Create a layout for your RecyclerView item that includes an ImageView:

   ```xml
   <ImageView
       android:id="@+id/imageView"
       android:layout_width="match_parent"
       android:layout_height="wrap_content"
       android:scaleType="centerCrop"
       android:layout_margin="8dp"/>
   ```

2. In your RecyclerView adapter, create a ViewHolder that has a reference to this ImageView:

   ```kotlin
   class MyViewHolder(itemView: View) : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(itemView) {
       val imageView: ImageView = itemView.findViewById(R.id.imageView)
   }
   ```

3. In your adapter's onCreateViewHolder() method, inflate the item layout:

   ```kotlin
   override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int): MyViewHolder {
       val itemView = LayoutInflater.from(parent.context)
           .inflate(R.layout.recycler_view_item, parent, false)
       return MyViewHolder(itemView)
   }
   ```

4. In your adapter's onBindViewHolder() method, retrieve the image at the specified location and set it to the ImageView:

   override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: MyViewHolder, position: Int) {
       val imageFile = File(imageLocations[position])
       val bitmap = BitmapFactory.decodeFile(imageFile.path)
       holder.imageView.setImageBitmap(bitmap)

```sql

FROM school s
JOIN school_library_operator o ON s.school_id = o.school_id
JOIN loan l ON o.operator_id = l.operator_id
WHERE YEAR(l.borrow_date) = year AND MONTH(l.borrow_date) = month
GROUP BY s.school_name;
```

2. For a given book category (user-selected), which authors belong to it and which teachers have borrowed books from that category in the last year?

```sql
SELECT a.author_name, t.teacher_name
FROM book_category c
JOIN book b ON c.category_id = b.category_id
JOIN book_author a ON b.book_id = a.book_id
JOIN loan l ON b.book_id = l.book_id
JOIN teacher t ON l.user_id = t.teacher_id
WHERE c.category_name = category AND YEAR(l.borrow_date) BETWEEN year(DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 1 YEAR)) AND year(NOW())
GROUP BY a.author_name, t.teacher_name;
```

3. Find young teachers (age < 40 years) who have borrowed the most books and the number of books.

```sql
SELECT t.teacher_name, COUNT(l.loan_id) as total_books
FROM teacher t
JOIN loan l ON t.teacher_id = l.user_id
WHERE TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, t.birthdate, CURDATE()) < 40
GROUP BY t.teacher_name
ORDER BY total_books DESC;
```

4. Find authors whose books have not been borrowed.

```sql

SELECT o.operator_name, COUNT(l.loan_id) as total_loans

WHERE YEAR(l.borrow_date) = year

```

6. Find the top-3 pairs that appeared in borrowings among field pairs (e.g., history and poetry) that are common in books.

```sql

FROM book b

JOIN book_category bc2 ON b.category_id_2 = bc2.category_id
JOIN loan l ON b.book_id = l.book_id

The best practice is to include the appropriate `chromedriver.exe` (or the correct driver executable for the target platform) with your Java project to keep dependencies organized and make it easier for others to run your application.

Here's how you can include the driver in your Java project and set the path programmatically:

1. Create a directory named `drivers` inside your `src/main/resources` folder (create the `resources` folder if it doesn't exist).

2. Place the `chromedriver.exe` file (or the appropriate driver for your platform) inside the `src/main/resources/drivers` directory. You should have a file structure similar to the following:

```
project-root
  ├── src
  │   ├── main
  │   │   ├── java
  │   │   │   └── <your_packages_and_classes>
  │   │   └── resources
  │   │       └── drivers
  │   │           └── chromedriver.exe
  │   └── test
  │       ├── java
  │       │   └── <your_package_and_test_classes>
  │       └── resources
  └── pom.xml
```

3. Modify your code to set the path programmatically by obtaining the resource URL from the class loader.

Replace this line:

```java
System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "path/to/your/chromedriver.exe");
```

with:

```java
URL chromeDriverResource = getClass().getClassLoader().getResource("drivers/chromedriver.exe");
System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", new File(chromeDriverResource.toURI()).getAbsolutePath());
```

Now, when you package your Java project, the driver will be included, and the resource's path will be set correctly.

It's important to note that the chromedriver and other WebDriver executables can be platform-dependent, so you should include the correct version for each target platform (Windows, macOS, Linux) and set the path based on the platform your application runs on. To make this process easier, you can use a library like the [WebDriverManager](https://github.com/bonigarcia/webdrivermanager) to manage WebDriver executables automatically for you.

You can try using the following methods to inspect and edit the form content of an Angular page:

1. Directly modifying the form value in HTML:

Open up the DevTools by right-clicking on the page and selecting "Inspect." Under the "Elements" tab, you can search and edit specific HTML elements, including form elements like `<input>`, `<textarea>`, and others.

2. Using `ng.probe`:

The `ng.probe` function returns a debug representation of an element, which includes the context, the component instance, and the element injector. You can access the component instance by running the following code in the console after selecting a targeted element in the "Elements" tab:

```javascript
const debugElement = ng.probe($0);
const componentInstance = debugElement.componentInstance;
```

You can then modify the form data on the component instance.

3. Querying the form control:

You can query the form control associated with the target form element, and then modify the form value by updating the control's value:

```javascript
const debugElement = ng.probe($0);
const formControl = debugElement.injector.get(ng.forms.FormControl);
formControl.setValue('new_value');
```

Note that `ng.getComponent()` is only available with Angular Language Service, which is installed in the form of a browser extension or an IDE extension. If you don't have the language service installed, you won't be able to use `ng.getComponent()`. However, the above methods should work for most cases where you want to edit the form content of an Angular page.

In OpenCascade, both Evolved and Pipe solids are used for creating more complex 3D shapes by sweeping a 2D profile along a path. However, they have some differences in the way they are created and the resulting geometry:

1. Evolved Solid: An Evolved solid is generated by sweeping a 2D profile along a straight or curved path while maintaining its orientation perpendicular to the path's tangential direction at every point. This creates a smooth transition from the starting profile to the end, resulting in a surface or solid with no twisting or deformation. Additionally, the Evolved solid allows for the profile to be scaled along the path, creating more complex shapes. Evolved solids are typically used in modeling extrusions, revolutions, and other simple sweeps where the profile's orientation remains consistent throughout the sweep.

2. Pipe Solid: A Pipe solid is created by sweeping a 2D profile along a path, allowing for the profile's orientation to be arbitrary with respect to the path's tangent. The profile can be rotated along the path to create twisted or more general 3D solids. This results in more complex and varied shapes, including solids with varying cross-sections, twists, and bends along their length. Pipe solids are commonly used in modeling cables, hoses, and more complex swept bodies where the orientation of the profile needs to be controlled along the path.

In summary, the primary difference between Evolved and Pipe solids in OpenCascade lies in how the 2D profile is oriented and swept along the path, resulting in different 3D geometries. The Evolved solid maintains a consistent orientation and potentially scales along the sweep while the Pipe solid allows for control of the profile's orientation, resulting in more complex and twisted shapes.

1. 对于 h265 编码的 25 fps 视频，我们可以根据帧速率计算 pts 和 dts 之间的间隔。我们知道，帧速率表示的是每秒钟显示的帧数。对于 25 fps 的视频，每秒钟有 25 帧，所以每帧之间的时间间隔是 1/25 = 0.04 秒。为了表示这个间隔，我们需要将其转换为以时间基（time_base）为单位的整数。通常情况下，对于 h265 编码的视频，时间基为 1/90000，所以 pts 和 dts 的间隔为：

   interval = 0.04 * 90000 = 3600
      
所以，您的估算是正确的，h265 25 fps 视频的 pts 和 dts 间隔为 3600。

2. 对于 AAC 编码的 44.1 KHz 音频，我们同样需要根据音频的采样率来计算 pts 和 dts 之间的间隔。AAC 音频通常使用 1024 个采样点（samples）作为一帧。对于 44.1 KHz 的音频，每秒钟有 44100 个采样点，所以每帧的时间间隔为：

   frame_duration = 1024 / 44100 ≈ 0.02322 秒

conversation.content: How to set up a backend server using Node.js react native

1. Set up Node.js 

The first step is to have Node.js installed on your computer. You can download it from the official website. Once you have installed it, you can check the version by running a simple command on the terminal or command prompt. 

2. Create a new project 

Create a new directory for your project and open the terminal or command prompt and navigate to the directory. Run the following command to initialize a new Node.js project.

```
npm init
```

This command will create a package.json file in your directory and prompt you to answer some questions about your project. 

3. Install the required packages 

You will need to install some packages to set up your backend server. Some of the essential packages are:

- Express.js: A popular web framework for Node.js
- Body-parser: A middleware to parse incoming request bodies
- Cors: A middleware to allow cross-origin resource sharing
- Mongoose: An Object Data Modeling (ODM) library for MongoDB

You can install these packages by running the following command.

```
npm install express body-parser cors mongoose
```

4. Create an Express.js app 

Next, create an Express.js server by creating a new file called `index.js` and adding the following code.

```javascript
const express = require('express')
const bodyParser = require('body-parser')
const cors = require('cors')

const app = express()

app.use(cors())
app.use(bodyParser.urlencoded({ extended: false }))
app.use(bodyParser.json())

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.send('Welcome to the backend server!')
})

const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000
app.listen(PORT, () => {
  console.log(`Server started on port ${PORT}`)
})
```

This code sets up an Express.js server, adds middleware for parsing incoming request bodies and enabling cross-origin resource sharing, sets up a route for the root endpoint, and starts the server on port 3000.

5. Connect to a MongoDB database 

You will need to have a MongoDB database set up. You can create a free account on the MongoDB Atlas website and create a new cluster. Once you have created a cluster, you can get the connection string by clicking on the Connect button and selecting Connect your application. 

Replace the connection string in the following code with your own connection string.

```javascript
const mongoose = require('mongoose')
mongoose.connect('mongodb://<username>:<password>@cluster0-shard-00-00.mongodb.net:27017,cluster0-shard-00-01.mongodb.net:27017,cluster0-shard-00-02.mongodb.net:27017/test?ssl=true&replicaSet=Cluster0-shard-0&authSource=admin', {
  useNewUrlParser: true,
  useUnifiedTopology: true
})

const db = mongoose.connection
db.on('error', console.error.bind(console, 'MongoDB connection error:'))
```

This code connects to a MongoDB database using the Mongoose library and logs an error message if the connection fails.

Now, you have set up a backend server using Node.js and Express.js which is connected to a MongoDB database. You can add more routes and functionality to your server based on your requirements.

conversation.content: How to setting mongo db react native

React Native is a mobile app development framework, and typically, you do not set up MongoDB directly on mobile devices. So, if you want to have a backend server with MongoDB to support your React Native app, you need to have a separate server, and you can use MongoDB on that server.

Here are the steps to set up MongoDB for a backend server that can support React Native apps:

1. Choose a cloud hosting service to host your MongoDB server. Some popular options include MongoDB Atlas, AWS, and Google Cloud. 

2. Create a MongoDB cluster: Log in to the cloud hosting service and create a new MongoDB cluster. Follow the instructions provided by the hosting service to create the cluster.

3. Create a new user: After creating the cluster, go to the Cluster dashboard and create a new user with a unique name and strong password. Note down these credentials.

4. Configure security: Set up security rules to restrict incoming traffic to your server. Add your IP address to the whitelist so that you can connect to the MongoDB server from your computer.

5. Connect to MongoDB server through your backend server: To connect to the MongoDB server through your backend server, you will require a MongoDB driver. A popular driver library is `mongoose`. You can install it using the command `npm install mongoose` in your Node.js environment.

6. Connect to MongoDB server in your Node.js code: In your Node.js code, use the following code to connect to the MongoDB server:

```javascript 
const mongoose = require('mongoose');

const mongoDbUrl = 'mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<cluster-url>/<database-name>?retryWrites=true&w=majority';

mongoose.connect(mongoDbUrl, {
  useNewUrlParser: true,
   useUnifiedTopology: true,
})
.then(() => console.log('Connected to MongoDB server.'))
.catch((error) => console.error(`Error connecting to MongoDB server - ${error}`));
```

Replace `<username>`, `<password>`, `<cluster-url>`, and `<database-name>` in the `mongoDbUrl` variable with your actual credentials. 

7. Test your connection: Run your Node.js server and confirm that it can connect to the MongoDB server. Test the connection by reading from or writing to MongoDB. 

With the MongoDB server set up and connected to the backend server, you can interact with the database through your back-end API endpoints which in turn can be used by your React Native app.

what is row and col in 2x2 matrix and how to better name member if use vec2f instances as referemce

A 2x2 matrix consists of two rows and two columns, represented as follows:

```
| a, b |
| c, d |
```

Each element (a, b, c, d) corresponds to a row and a column. For example, a is in row 1 and column 1, b is in row 1 and column 2, c is in row 2 and column 1, and d is in row 2 and column 2.

If you want to use vec2f instances as members of the 2x2 matrix, you can represent the matrix as two vec2f instances, where each vec2f represents a row or a column of the matrix. Here are two alternatives for naming the members:

1. If you want to represent each vec2f as a row:

```cpp
struct mat2f {
    vec2f row1; // First row: | a, b |
    vec2f row2; // Second row: | c, d |
};
```

2. If you want to represent each vec2f as a column:

```cpp
struct mat2f {
    vec2f col1; // First column: | a, c |
    vec2f col2; // Second column: | b, d |
};
```

Choose the representation (row or column) that makes the most sense for your use case and is more convenient for your operations, such as matrix multiplication or transformations. For example, if you are using a column-major representation for combining transformations, representing vec2f instances as columns might be more suitable.

When you want to insert data in the second table that has a foreign key referencing the primary key of the first table (which has an auto-increment feature), you will need to provide the value of the primary key from the first table that you want to reference.

Here are the steps to do this:

1. Insert data into the first table: Since the first table has an auto-increment feature, you won't need to provide the primary key value while inserting, as it will be auto-generated by the database.

```sql
INSERT INTO first_table (column1, column2)
VALUES ('value1', 'value2');
```

2. Get the primary key value of the inserted row in the first table: After inserting the data into the first table, you will need to retrieve the auto-generated primary key value. It usually depends on the database server you are using. For example, in MySQL you can use `LAST_INSERT_ID()`, while in SQL Server you can use `SCOPE_IDENTITY()`.

3. Insert data into the second table: Finally, you can use the primary key value from the first table as a foreign key value while inserting data into the second table.

```sql
INSERT INTO second_table (foreign_key, column1, column2)
VALUES (primary_key_value_from_first_table, 'value1', 'value2');
```

Make sure to replace the primary_key_value_from_first_table with the actual value retrieved in step 2.

Sure, here are the steps to install Firebase for React Native:

1. Install Firebase CLI by running the following command in your terminal: 

```
npm install -g firebase-tools
```

2. Create a new project on Firebase Console (https://console.firebase.google.com/) with the desired name and follow the setup instructions.

3. Make sure that you have a Firebase project added to your Firebase CLI. You can check this by running the following command in your terminal:

```
firebase projects:list
```

If you don't see the desired project listed, add it by running the following command:

```
firebase use --add
```

4. Initialize Firebase in your React Native project by running the following commands:

```
firebase init
```

This will prompt you with a series of questions. Select `Functions` and `Hosting` while skipping the `Database`, `Firestore`, and `Storage` options. You can accept the default values for the remaining questions.

5. Install the required Firebase libraries in your project. Run the following command in your project directory:

```
npm install firebase @react-native-firebase/app @react-native-firebase/functions @react-native-firebase/auth
```

6. Link the Firebase libraries by running the following command:

```
react-native link @react-native-firebase/app
```
And similarly for `@react-native-firebase/functions` and `@react-native-firebase/auth`.

7. Add the required Firebase dependencies to the `android/app/build.gradle` file. Add the following dependencies to the dependencies section:

```
implementation "com.google.firebase:firebase-auth:19.3.2"
implementation "com.google.firebase:firebase-functions:20.0.0"
```

8. Add the following line to your `android/app/src/main/java/com/your_project/MainApplication.java` file, within the `getPackages()` method:

```java
import io.invertase.firebase.app.ReactNativeFirebaseAppPackage;

new ReactNativeFirebaseAppPackage()
```

9. Download your Firebase configuration file `google-services.json` from your Firebase Console and place it inside the `android/app` directory.

10. Build and run your project. You can do this by running the following commands:

```
cd android && ./gradlew clean && cd ..
react-native run-android
```
